lessons.plain: Booting is the relay race a computer runs from power-on to a usable system. The firmware built into the motherboard wakes first and hands off to a bootloader, a small program whose job is to find and start the operating system. On most Linux systems the bootloader is GRUB. GRUB loads the kernel, the core of Linux. The kernel then starts systemd, the first program, which brings up everything else. systemd aims at a goal state called a target, such as 'text-only server' or 'full desktop'. Think of targets as destinations on a train line: you choose where to stop, and every station before it gets visited.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server normally starts with a graphical desktop, but it is used only remotely over the command line. What do you think you would change so it starts in text-only mode, and would that change be made in the bootloader or in the program that starts services?
lessons.teach:
The Linux boot process is the chain of hand-offs from power-on to a working system. First, firmware (BIOS, or its modern replacement UEFI) tests the hardware and finds a bootloader. The bootloader is GRUB (GRand Unified Bootloader, version 2). It shows a menu, then loads the kernel plus an initramfs, a small temporary root filesystem holding the drivers needed to reach the real disk. The kernel mounts the real root filesystem and starts systemd as process ID 1, the parent of all other processes.

systemd groups services into units, and a target is a unit that names a system state by pulling in other units. Common targets: multi-user.target (networking, text logins, no desktop), graphical.target (multi-user plus a desktop), rescue.target (single user, minimal services, root filesystem mounted), and emergency.target (even less, root often mounted read-only). default.target is a link pointing at whichever target boots normally.

This works because each stage only needs to know how to start the next one, so problems can be isolated by stage.

Worked example: make a server boot to text mode. Run systemctl get-default; it prints graphical.target. Run systemctl set-default multi-user.target; systemd repoints the default.target link. Run systemctl isolate multi-user.target to switch now without rebooting; the desktop stops. On next boot, systemd reaches multi-user.target. For a one-time rescue boot instead, press e at the GRUB menu, add systemd.unit=rescue.target to the line starting with linux, and press Ctrl+X to boot; this edit is not saved.

GRUB's permanent settings, such as the default menu entry or timeout, live in /etc/default/grub. You then regenerate the real configuration with update-grub on Debian-family systems or grub2-mkconfig -o followed by the output path on Red Hat-family systems.

Common mistake: editing grub.cfg directly. It is a generated file, so the next kernel update or regeneration silently overwrites your change, and a server you expected to boot a certain way does not.

questions.prompt: A clinic's lab server runs a Red Hat-family Linux. The admin wants the GRUB menu to wait 3 seconds instead of the current timeout, and wants the change to survive kernel updates. Step 1: open /etc/default/grub and change the timeout setting to 3. Step 2: ??? Step 3: reboot; the GRUB menu now waits 3 seconds, and the setting persists after the next kernel update. What is Step 2?
choices: Open grub.cfg and change its timeout line to 3 as well
Run systemctl set-default so systemd records the new timeout
Run update-grub so the new timeout is written into the real configuration
Run grub2-mkconfig -o followed by the output path to regenerate the real configuration
questions.why: On Red Hat-family systems, grub2-mkconfig -o with the output path regenerates the real GRUB configuration from /etc/default/grub (update-grub is the Debian-family command).

questions.prompt: During boot, GRUB loads the kernel along with an initramfs. What is the initramfs?
choices: A small temporary root filesystem holding the drivers needed to reach the real disk
The systemd unit that names the normal boot state
The generated GRUB menu file that lists kernel entries
The firmware that tests hardware and locates the bootloader
questions.why: The initramfs is a small temporary root filesystem that gives the kernel the drivers it needs before it can mount the real root filesystem.

questions.prompt: At a shipping company, a shared workstation normally boots to a desktop (graphical.target). A technician wants it in text-only mode with networking right now, without rebooting, and without changing what it boots to next time. Which command fits?
choices: systemctl isolate rescue.target
systemctl isolate multi-user.target
systemctl set-default rescue.target
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
questions.why: isolate switches the running system to the named target immediately without repointing default.target, and multi-user.target gives networking and text logins without a desktop.

questions.prompt: An admin at a university changed the default kernel entry by editing grub.cfg directly. It worked for weeks, then after a kernel update the server booted a different entry. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The kernel update reset default.target to graphical.target
grub.cfg is a generated file, so regeneration during the update overwrote the manual edit
The initramfs was rebuilt and replaced the GRUB menu
systemd, as process ID 1, reverted the bootloader settings at startup
questions.why: grub.cfg is generated from /etc/default/grub, so regenerating it (as happens on kernel updates) silently discards direct edits.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the stages a Linux machine goes through from power-on to a login prompt, where GRUB and systemd targets fit, and one limit or tradeoff of the ways to change what it boots into.
lessons.modelAnswer: Power-on starts the firmware, BIOS or UEFI, which finds the bootloader, GRUB. GRUB loads the kernel and an initramfs, a small temporary filesystem with the drivers needed to reach the real disk. The kernel mounts the root filesystem and starts systemd as process 1. systemd then works toward a target, a named system state: multi-user for a text server, graphical for a desktop, rescue or emergency for repair. default.target decides the normal one, and systemctl set-default changes it permanently while systemctl isolate switches right now. The tradeoff: adding systemd.unit=rescue.target at the GRUB menu is quick but lasts for one boot only, while permanent GRUB changes belong in /etc/default/grub followed by regenerating the config. Editing grub.cfg directly gets overwritten on the next kernel update, so the fix quietly disappears.
rubricPoints: Names the order: firmware, GRUB, kernel with initramfs, systemd as PID 1, target.
Defines a target as a named system state and gives multi-user versus graphical.
Mentions rescue or emergency targets for repair.
Distinguishes set-default (persistent) from isolate or a GRUB menu edit (immediate or one-time).
Notes GRUB settings go in /etc/default/grub and must be regenerated, not edited in grub.cfg.

suggested.rationale: No current mission touches booting, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios such as a server stuck before login or one that boots to the wrong target builds the stage-by-stage diagnosis the exam expects.

lessons.plain: A package is a bundle containing a program, its settings files and a note listing what else it needs to run. A package manager is the tool that installs, updates, lists and removes those bundles for you, much like an app store on a phone. Different Linux families use different managers: Debian and Ubuntu use apt, Red Hat style systems use dnf (older ones use yum), and Arch uses pacman. Underneath, rpm handles individual Red Hat package files. Knowing which family a system belongs to tells you which tool to reach for.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you install a program by hand from a single downloaded file, and that program needs three other libraries you do not have, what do you think happens, and how might a smarter tool avoid the problem?
lessons.teach:
A package manager installs, upgrades, queries and removes software packages. A package is an archive of files plus metadata: name, version and dependencies, meaning other packages it needs. A repository is an online collection of packages with an index, a catalogue of what is available. Low-level tools work on one package file and do not fetch anything: rpm on Red Hat family systems, dpkg on Debian family. High-level tools read repositories, resolve dependencies automatically and call the low-level tool: apt (Debian, Ubuntu), dnf (Fedora, RHEL 8 and later; yum is its older predecessor with similar commands) and pacman (Arch, which does both jobs itself).

Worked example: you must install nginx on an unfamiliar server. Step 1, read /etc/os-release; it says ID_LIKE="rhel fedora", so this is Red Hat family. Step 2, run dnf install nginx. Step 3, dnf checks its repository index, finds nginx needs extra libraries, lists them, and asks to confirm. Step 4, it downloads all of them, checks their signatures, and hands them to rpm to install. Step 5, confirm with rpm -q nginx. On Ubuntu the same job is apt update (refresh the index) then apt install nginx; on Arch, pacman -Syu nginx.

Useful queries: rpm -qa lists every installed package, rpm -qf /path tells you which package owns a file, dpkg -l lists packages on Debian family, and pacman -Q does so on Arch.

A common mistake is installing a downloaded file directly with rpm -i or dpkg -i. These do not fetch dependencies, so the install fails or leaves a half-configured package. Another is skipping apt update, so apt works from a stale index and cannot find current versions. On a running server, bypassing the high-level tool can leave broken libraries that stop services from starting after the next reboot or upgrade.

questions.prompt: A technician at a regional bus company finds an unfamiliar program at /usr/sbin/chronyd on a server and needs to know which installed package it came from. Step 1: they read /etc/os-release, which shows ID="fedora", so this is a Red Hat family system. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the output names the package chrony, so they now know which software put the file there. Step 4: they run rpm -q chrony to confirm the package is installed and see its version. Which command belongs in Step 2?
choices: rpm -qf /usr/sbin/chronyd
dnf install chrony
dpkg -l chronyd
pacman -Q chronyd
questions.why: On a Red Hat family system, rpm -qf followed by a file path reports which installed package owns that file, which is exactly the question being asked.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a low-level package tool such as rpm or dpkg and a high-level tool such as dnf or apt?
choices: The high-level tool reads repositories and resolves dependencies automatically, then hands packages to the low-level tool, which works on a single package file and fetches nothing.
The low-level tool downloads packages faster because it skips signature checks.
Both do the same job, but the high-level tool only works on Arch.
The low-level tool reads repositories and resolves dependencies, then calls the high-level tool to unpack files.
questions.why: Low-level tools act on one package file without fetching anything, while high-level tools consult repository indexes, pull in dependencies and call the low-level tool to do the install.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a small design studio logs into a freshly built Ubuntu server and runs apt install htop. apt reports it cannot find a current version of the package, even though htop is available in Ubuntu's repositories. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Download the htop .deb file and install it with dpkg -i
Run pacman -Syu htop instead
Run apt update to refresh the repository index, then run apt install htop again
Switch to rpm -i htop, since apt cannot install it
questions.why: apt works from a local copy of the repository index, so if that index is stale it cannot find current versions until apt update refreshes it.

questions.prompt: At a hospital records office, an administrator installs a downloaded package file on a Debian server with dpkg -i. The file needs two libraries that are not installed. What is the most likely result, and what risk does it create for the running server?
choices: dpkg automatically downloads the two libraries from the repository, so there is no risk.
The package installs normally, and dpkg only shows a warning the next time apt update runs.
The install fails or leaves a half-configured package, and missing or broken libraries can stop services from starting after the next reboot or upgrade.
dpkg converts the file into an rpm package and installs it with no dependencies needed.
questions.why: dpkg works on one file and does not fetch dependencies, so missing libraries cause a failed or half-configured install that can break services later.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a low-level package tool like rpm and a high-level one like dnf or apt, how you would pick the right one on an unfamiliar server, and one limit or risk of using the low-level tool directly.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every distribution family has its own package manager, so first I check /etc/os-release to see whether the box is Debian-like, Red Hat-like or Arch. Then I know whether to use apt, dnf (or yum on older systems) or pacman. Those high-level tools talk to repositories, which are catalogues of packages, work out dependencies, the other packages something needs, download everything, verify signatures and install it all. Under the hood they call a low-level tool, rpm or dpkg, which only handles a single package file already on disk. The low-level tool is still handy for queries, like rpm -qa to list everything or rpm -qf to find which package owns a file. The risk of installing with rpm or dpkg directly is that dependencies are not fetched, so you can get failed or half-broken installs that stop services working later.
rubricPoints: Identifies the distribution family first, for example via /etc/os-release.
Maps families to tools: apt for Debian/Ubuntu, dnf or yum for Red Hat, pacman for Arch.
States that high-level tools use repositories and resolve dependencies automatically.
States that rpm and dpkg work on single local files and do not fetch dependencies.
Names a query use such as listing installed packages or finding a file's owner.
Names a risk such as broken dependencies or a stale index.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises package managers, so reasoning through exam-style 'unfamiliar server, which command' scenarios best builds the distro-to-tool mapping.

lessons.plain: Linux keeps every file in one big tree that starts at a single top folder called root, written as a slash. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) is an agreed layout saying which folder holds what: settings in one place, logs in another, user files in a third. Mounting is how a separate disk joins that tree: you pick an empty folder and tell the system that this folder now shows the disk's contents. Think of a building with fixed room labels; mounting adds a new wing through one doorway. Unmounting closes that doorway so the disk can be removed safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: Windows gives a new USB drive its own letter, such as D:. Linux has no drive letters. Where do you think the files on a newly attached disk show up, and what would have to happen first?
lessons.teach:
The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) is a published convention for where files belong on a Linux system, so any admin can find things on an unfamiliar server. Everything hangs from / (the root directory). Key branches: /etc holds system configuration files; /var holds data that changes while running, such as logs in /var/log; /home holds users' personal folders; /usr holds installed programs and libraries; /boot holds the kernel and boot files; /tmp holds temporary files; /dev holds device files, which are special files that represent hardware such as disks (/dev/sdb1 is partition 1 of the second disk); /proc and /sys are virtual, meaning the kernel generates their contents on the fly; /mnt and /media are conventional places to attach extra storage.

Mounting attaches a filesystem (the structure that organizes data on a partition) to a directory, called the mount point. Afterwards, reading that directory reads the disk. Unmounting detaches it and flushes pending writes. The file /etc/fstab lists mounts to make automatically at boot. Tools: mount and umount do the work; lsblk shows disks and partitions; findmnt and df -h show what is mounted where and how full it is.

Worked example: lsblk shows an unmounted /dev/sdb1. Run mkdir /mnt/data to create a mount point, then mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data. Now ls /mnt/data lists the disk's files, and df -h shows /dev/sdb1 on /mnt/data. When finished, run umount /mnt/data. If it reports "target is busy", a process or your own shell is still using it; cd elsewhere and retry.

Common mistake: copying files into a mount point while nothing is mounted there. They land on the root disk and become hidden once the real disk is mounted on top. On a running server, the same happens when a data disk fails to mount at boot: an application writes to /var/lib/app on the root disk instead, which can fill root and stop the system. A typo in /etc/fstab can also halt booting, so test new entries with mount -a before rebooting.

questions.prompt: At a small dental clinic, an admin wants a new scanner-archive disk to attach automatically at every boot. Here is the work so far. Step 1: lsblk shows a partition /dev/sdd1 that is not mounted anywhere. Step 2: mkdir /srv/xrays creates an empty directory to act as the mount point (the directory a filesystem gets attached to). Step 3: the admin adds a line to /etc/fstab, the file listing mounts to make at boot, that attaches /dev/sdd1 to /srv/xrays. Step 4: ??? Step 5: findmnt shows /dev/sdd1 on /srv/xrays, and only then does the admin schedule a reboot. What is Step 4?
choices: Run umount /srv/xrays so the new fstab line gets flushed to disk
Run mount -a so every fstab entry is mounted now and any typo shows up before a reboot
Run lsblk again, which saves the new fstab line as permanent
Reboot right away, because fstab entries are only read during boot and cannot be tested beforehand
questions.why: mount -a applies the fstab entries immediately, so a mistake that could halt booting is caught while the system is still running.

questions.prompt: A city library hires you to look after a Linux server that runs its web catalogue. Following the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (the shared convention for where files belong), which pair of directories should you check first for the web server's configuration files and for its log files?
choices: /usr for configuration and /tmp for logs
/boot for configuration and /proc for logs
/etc for configuration and /var/log for logs
/home for configuration and /dev for logs
questions.why: /etc holds system configuration files, and /var holds data that changes while the system runs, with logs kept in /var/log.

questions.prompt: A photo studio's server should mount its data disk, /dev/sdc1, on /srv/photos at boot. One morning the disk failed to mount, but the upload app kept saving pictures into /srv/photos all day. The admin then mounted /dev/sdc1 on /srv/photos, and the day's uploads no longer appear in that directory. What best explains this?
choices: The kernel moved the files to /tmp when the mount failed
Mounting a filesystem erases whatever was in the mount point before
The files were written to the root disk under /srv/photos and are now hidden beneath the mounted disk
The files went straight onto /dev/sdc1 but are unreadable until the disk is mounted twice
questions.why: With nothing mounted, /srv/photos was just a directory on the root disk, and mounting the real disk on top hides those files without deleting them.

questions.prompt: You copied reports onto a USB stick mounted at /media/usbstick. Your shell is still sitting in /media/usbstick/reports. You run umount /media/usbstick and it replies "target is busy". What should you do next?
choices: Change your shell to a directory outside the stick, such as your home folder, then run umount again
Run mount -a so the system re-reads fstab and frees the stick
Delete the /media/usbstick directory so the mount is released
Pull the stick out now, since the copy command already finished
questions.why: "Target is busy" means something is still using the mount, here your own shell, so moving elsewhere lets umount detach it and flush pending writes safely.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is and what mounting does, then describe one risk or limitation of how mounting works and how you would check for it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is a shared convention for where things live on Linux, all under one tree starting at /. Config goes in /etc, changing data and logs in /var, user files in /home, programs in /usr, device files in /dev, and /proc and /sys are virtual views generated by the kernel. Because the layout is predictable, I can find logs or config on a server I have never seen. Mounting attaches a filesystem on a device, like /dev/sdb1, to a directory called a mount point, so that directory shows the disk's contents; umount detaches it and flushes writes. Persistent mounts go in /etc/fstab. The risk is that a mount point is just an ordinary directory: if the disk is not mounted, writes land on the root disk and get hidden later, possibly filling root. I check with findmnt or df -h before trusting a path, and test fstab changes with mount -a.
rubricPoints: Defines the FHS as a standard layout rooted at / and names several directories with their purpose.
Explains that mounting attaches a device's filesystem to a directory called a mount point.
Mentions unmounting, including that a busy mount point cannot be unmounted.
Notes /etc/fstab for mounts at boot and the danger of errors in it.
Names the hidden-files or root-fills-up risk when a disk is not mounted.
Names a command such as findmnt, df -h or lsblk to verify mounts.

suggested.rationale: Navigating an unfamiliar server makes the learner use the standard directory layout and inspect what is mounted, which is exactly this objective.

lessons.plain: A hard disk is like a large plot of land. Partitioning divides it into fixed fields with fences. LVM (Logical Volume Manager) works more like a land bank: it pools fields from one or more disks and hands out plots that can be enlarged later without rebuilding fences. A filesystem is the filing system laid over each plot. It decides how files are named, stored and found again. Linux offers several filesystems. ext4 is the dependable all-rounder. xfs is built for big files and heavy workloads. btrfs adds snapshots, which are instant copies of a moment in time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's data area is full and you want to give it 10 GB more from a spare pool of disk space without rebooting. Do you think making the storage container bigger is enough on its own, or must something inside it also be told to grow?
lessons.teach:
A partition is a fixed slice of a physical disk, recorded in a partition table at the start of that disk. The older table format, MBR (Master Boot Record), allows four primary partitions and disks up to about 2 TB. The newer GPT (GUID Partition Table) allows many partitions and much larger disks. Tools such as fdisk, gdisk and parted edit these tables, and lsblk shows the layout.

Plain partitions are hard to resize, so LVM (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer. A physical volume (PV) is a disk or partition handed to LVM. A volume group (VG) pools one or more PVs into a single store of space. A logical volume (LV) is a slice carved from the VG. It behaves like a partition but can grow, shrink or span several disks. This works because LVM maps the LV's blocks onto any free space in the pool, so the LV need not be contiguous or sit on one disk. The commands pvs, vgs and lvs list each layer.

A filesystem is the structure that organises files inside a partition or LV. ext4 is the long-standing default on Debian and Ubuntu. It is mature and can grow, and it can shrink only while unmounted. xfs is the Red Hat family default and is strong with large files and parallel writes. It grows while mounted but can never shrink. btrfs is copy-on-write, meaning changed data goes to new blocks instead of overwriting old ones. That design gives cheap snapshots, data checksums and built-in multi-disk pooling.

Worked example: /var is a full xfs LV, and vgs shows 20 GB free in the VG. First, lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/var grows the LV. Second, xfs_growfs /var grows the filesystem to fill it. Running df -h now shows 10 GB more, with no unmount. For ext4, step two would be resize2fs instead, and lvextend -r performs both steps at once.

Common mistake: growing the LV but forgetting the filesystem. In that case df still shows the old size, and the service keeps failing with 'No space left on device'.

questions.prompt: A small design studio runs Ubuntu. Its media share lives on an ext4 logical volume (an LVM slice that acts like a partition) mounted at /srv/media, and uploads are failing. The admin works through it. Step 1: df -h shows /srv/media at 100% use. Step 2: vgs shows 40 GB free in the volume group vg_media. Step 3: lvextend -L +25G /dev/vg_media/media grows the logical volume by 25 GB. Step 4: ??? Step 5: df -h now shows /srv/media about 25 GB larger, and uploads work again. What is Step 4?
choices: Run xfs_growfs /srv/media so the filesystem expands to fill the larger volume
Do nothing; df -h picks up the new size as soon as lvextend finishes
Unmount /srv/media and use fdisk to add a new partition for the extra space
Run resize2fs /dev/vg_media/media so the ext4 filesystem expands to fill the larger volume
questions.why: Growing the logical volume does not grow the filesystem inside it, and for ext4 the tool that grows the filesystem is resize2fs (xfs_growfs is only for xfs).

questions.prompt: A research lab is setting up a Linux file server. They want to take cheap, frequent snapshots of project data, have the filesystem checksum data to catch corruption, and pool several disks inside the filesystem itself. Which filesystem fits best?
choices: Any of them, because snapshots and checksums are provided by the partition table
ext4, because it is mature and is the Debian and Ubuntu default
xfs, because it handles large files and parallel writes well
btrfs, because its copy-on-write design gives snapshots, checksums and multi-disk pooling
questions.why: btrfs is copy-on-write, meaning changed data goes to new blocks, and that design is what gives it cheap snapshots, data checksums and built-in multi-disk pooling.

questions.prompt: On a Red Hat family server, an admin gave a logging volume far too much space: an 800 GB xfs filesystem on a logical volume that only ever uses about 100 GB. They want to shrink it to 300 GB to free space in the volume group. What is true?
choices: They can shrink it while mounted, because xfs resizes online in both directions
They can shrink it, but only after unmounting it first
They cannot shrink it in place, because an xfs filesystem can grow but can never shrink
They only need lvreduce, because the filesystem shrinks along with the volume
questions.why: xfs can be grown while mounted but cannot be shrunk at all; shrinking only while unmounted is a property of ext4, not xfs.

questions.prompt: A hosting company installs a new 6 TB disk and wants to split it into seven partitions (fixed slices of the disk recorded in a partition table). Which partition table format should they use?
choices: MBR, using four primary partitions and splitting each one later
GPT, because it supports many partitions and disks far larger than 2 TB
Either format, because the partition table does not limit size or count
MBR, because it is the older and more widely supported format
questions.why: MBR is limited to four primary partitions and disks up to about 2 TB, while GPT allows many partitions and much larger disks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how partitions, LVM and the filesystem stack on top of each other, and name one limit that should influence whether they pick xfs or ext4 for a new volume.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of it as three layers. At the bottom, partitions cut a disk into fixed slices using an MBR or GPT partition table. LVM sits on top. Disks or partitions become physical volumes, those are pooled into a volume group, and we carve logical volumes out of the pool. Logical volumes can grow or span disks because LVM maps them onto any free space. On top of each LV goes a filesystem, which actually organises the files. Resizing therefore takes two steps: grow the LV, then grow the filesystem with xfs_growfs or resize2fs, or use lvextend -r. The key tradeoff is that xfs handles large files and heavy parallel writes well and grows while mounted, but it can never shrink. ext4 can shrink, though only while unmounted. If the volume might need to give space back later, ext4 is safer. btrfs adds snapshots and checksums through copy-on-write.
rubricPoints: Partitions are fixed slices of a disk defined in an MBR or GPT partition table.
LVM pools physical volumes into a volume group and carves resizable logical volumes from it.
A filesystem organises files inside a partition or logical volume and must be grown separately after the LV grows.
xfs can grow online but cannot shrink, while ext4 can shrink only when unmounted.
btrfs uses copy-on-write to provide snapshots and checksums.

suggested.rationale: No current mission makes the learner build or resize LVM volumes, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios is the most useful practice. Good scenarios include choosing a filesystem, growing a full volume, and spotting the forgotten filesystem-resize step.

lessons.plain: On most modern Linux systems, a program called systemd acts like a building manager for background programs, called services, such as a web server or a database. It starts them when the machine boots, restarts them if asked, and keeps a logbook of what each one said and did. You talk to this manager with two command-line tools. systemctl is how you give orders and ask for status: start, stop, restart, or switch on automatic start at boot. journalctl is how you read the logbook to find out why a service is unhappy.
lessons.guessPrompt: You start a web server service on a Linux machine and it runs fine, but after the machine reboots the service is not running. What do you think you forgot to tell the system?
lessons.teach:
systemd is the first program Linux starts, and it manages everything after it. Each thing it manages is described by a unit, a small configuration file; a service unit (name ending in .service) describes one background program, often called a daemon. systemctl is the command for controlling units, and journalctl reads the journal, which is systemd's central, searchable log store.

The core systemctl verbs are start (run it now), stop (end it now), restart (stop then start), reload (re-read its configuration without a full stop, if the program supports it), and status (state, process ID, and the last few log lines). Separately, enable makes a service start automatically at boot and disable removes that. Running is about now, and enabled is about the next boot. If you edit a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload so systemd reads the change.

Worked example: users report the site is down. Step 1, run systemctl status nginx and see "failed" in red. Step 2, run journalctl -u nginx (the -u option filters to one unit), adding -e to jump to the end or -f to follow new lines live. The last entries show a syntax error in a configuration file. Step 3, fix the file. Step 4, run systemctl restart nginx, then check status again and see "active (running)". Step 5, run systemctl is-enabled nginx to confirm it will survive a reboot, and use systemctl enable nginx if it will not.

Useful journalctl filters also include -b (this boot only), --since "1 hour ago", and -p err (errors and worse).

The most common mistake is to treat start and enable as the same thing. Starting a service without enabling it works until the next reboot or maintenance window, and then the service silently stays down. Enabling it without starting it leaves it down until the machine reboots. systemctl enable --now does both at once.

questions.prompt: At a small veterinary clinic, an administrator changes the unit file for a backup daemon called vetbackup.service so that it restarts automatically after a crash. The file lives at /etc/systemd/system/vetbackup.service. Step 1: save the edited unit file. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: run systemctl restart vetbackup. Step 4: run systemctl status vetbackup and confirm it shows "active (running)" with the new behaviour in effect. Which command belongs in Step 2?
choices: journalctl -u vetbackup -f
systemctl reload vetbackup
systemctl enable vetbackup
systemctl daemon-reload
questions.why: After editing a unit file, systemctl daemon-reload makes systemd read the changed file. reload only asks the program to re-read its own configuration, and it does not refresh the unit file.

questions.prompt: On a print server at a law firm, a technician ran systemctl start cupsd on Monday and printing worked all week. After Saturday's scheduled reboot, printing is down, and systemctl status shows the service is inactive. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The service was not reloaded after it started
The unit file needs systemctl restart to persist
The journal filled up and stopped the service
The service was started but never enabled
questions.why: start only runs a service now. Without enable, it does not come back after a reboot, so it silently stays down.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to see only error-level and worse log entries from the redis unit, limited to the current boot. Which command does that?
choices: systemctl status redis -p err
journalctl -b -e --since redis
journalctl -u redis -b -p err
journalctl -u redis -f -e
questions.why: -u limits the output to one unit, -b limits it to this boot, and -p err shows errors and worse.

questions.prompt: A new metrics agent, statsd.service, was just installed on a monitoring host. The admin ran only systemctl enable statsd, and no dashboards are receiving data. Which single command would have made it run immediately and also start at every boot?
choices: systemctl daemon-reload statsd
systemctl restart statsd
systemctl enable --now statsd
systemctl is-enabled statsd
questions.why: enable alone only affects the next boot. enable --now enables the service and starts it at once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would investigate and fix a service that has stopped working, using systemctl and journalctl, and describe one limit or tradeoff, such as start versus enable or restart versus reload.
lessons.modelAnswer: systemd manages background services, and each service is defined by a unit file. I'd first run systemctl status on the service. That shows whether it's active or failed, plus its last few log lines. For the full story I'd run journalctl -u with the unit name, using -e to jump to the newest entries or -b to limit output to this boot. Once the log shows the cause, I fix it and run systemctl restart, then check status again. If I edited the unit file itself, I run daemon-reload first. Finally, I check is-enabled, because start only affects now while enable controls boot. A service that's started but not enabled will vanish after a reboot. One tradeoff is that restart briefly drops connections. Reload is gentler, but only if the program supports re-reading its config.
rubricPoints: Uses systemctl status to see the service state before acting.
Uses journalctl -u to read that service's logs and find the cause.
Restarts or reloads after the fix and confirms with status.
Distinguishes start or running now from enable or start at boot.
Names a tradeoff such as restart versus reload, or the need for daemon-reload after editing a unit.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose a broken service, fix it, and restart it from the shell, which exercises systemctl and journalctl directly.

lessons.plain: The kernel is the core program of Linux that talks directly to hardware and manages memory, processes and networking. Kernel modules are add-on pieces of the kernel, such as a driver for a network card, that can be loaded or unloaded while the system runs, without rebooting. Kernel parameters are adjustable settings inside the running kernel, like whether the machine forwards network traffic between interfaces. Think of the kernel as a car engine: modules are parts you can bolt on or remove, and parameters are the dials on the dashboard. Some dial changes last only until you switch the engine off unless you write them down.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you change a setting inside the running Linux kernel with a command, but never save it to any file, what do you think happens to that setting after the machine reboots?
lessons.teach:
A kernel module is a file of kernel code (ending in .ko) that can be loaded into the running kernel on demand, usually a hardware driver or filesystem support. lsmod lists the modules currently loaded. modinfo shows a module's description, file path, dependencies and options. modprobe loads a module by name and automatically loads any other modules it depends on; modprobe -r removes it. insmod and rmmod also load and remove modules, but insmod needs a full file path and does not resolve dependencies. To stop a module from ever loading, add a line such as "blacklist pcspkr" to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/. To load one at every boot, list its name in a file under /etc/modules-load.d/.

A kernel parameter is a tunable value in the running kernel. Linux exposes them as small files under /proc/sys, a virtual directory that lives in memory, not on disk. The sysctl command reads and writes them using dotted names, so net.ipv4.ip_forward maps to /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward.

Worked example, turning a server into a router. Step 1: run sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward and see 0, meaning off. Step 2: run sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1; forwarding works immediately. Step 3: to survive a reboot, write net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 into a file such as /etc/sysctl.d/99-forward.conf (or /etc/sysctl.conf). Step 4: run sysctl --system (or sysctl -p for a single file) to apply saved files now and confirm there are no typos.

Common mistake: stopping after step 2. sysctl -w and echo into /proc/sys change memory only, so the setting silently reverts at the next reboot. In a running system that means a router stops routing, or a security hardening setting quietly disappears, exactly when nobody is watching. The same trap applies to modules: modprobe loads one now, but only a modules-load.d entry brings it back after boot.

questions.prompt: A public library connects a USB serial adapter to a workstation. The adapter needs the kernel module ftdi_sio, and it must work now and after every reboot. Step 1: the technician runs lsmod and finds no ftdi_sio line, so the module is not loaded. Step 2: running modinfo ftdi_sio shows that the module depends on another module, usbserial. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the technician writes the line ftdi_sio into /etc/modules-load.d/serial.conf so the module loads again at every boot. Which command belongs in Step 3 to load the module immediately, along with what it depends on?
choices: insmod ftdi_sio
rmmod usbserial
modprobe ftdi_sio
echo blacklist ftdi_sio > /etc/modprobe.d/serial.conf
questions.why: modprobe loads a module by name and automatically loads its dependencies, such as usbserial, while insmod needs a full file path and does not resolve dependencies.

questions.prompt: A kernel parameter is a tunable value in the running kernel. Linux exposes these values as small files in a virtual directory. A web hosting company wants to inspect the kernel parameter that sysctl calls kernel.pid_max. Which file holds that value?
choices: /proc/sys/kernel.pid_max
/etc/modprobe.d/kernel.pid_max
/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max
/etc/sysctl.d/kernel/pid_max
questions.why: sysctl's dotted names map to paths under /proc/sys, with each dot becoming a slash, so kernel.pid_max is /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max.

questions.prompt: At an accounting firm, an engineer hardens a server by running echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_syncookies. A check confirms the value is 1. After a scheduled reboot the next month, the value is back to 0. What is the most likely reason?
choices: sysctl --system must be run after every echo, or the change is ignored.
/proc/sys lives in memory, so the change was never saved to a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ or /etc/sysctl.conf.
Writing to /proc/sys only works for parameters whose names begin with kernel.
The tcp_syncookies module was blacklisted in /etc/modprobe.d/.
questions.why: Writing into /proc/sys changes only the running kernel's memory, so the setting reverts at reboot unless it is also saved in a sysctl configuration file.

questions.prompt: A school computer lab wants to make sure the kernel module named floppy never loads on its machines, including after a reboot. Which action does this?
choices: Run modprobe -r floppy once on each machine
Run sysctl -w floppy=0 and then sysctl --system
Add the line blacklist floppy to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/
List floppy in a file under /etc/modules-load.d/
questions.why: A blacklist line in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ stops the module from being loaded, whereas modprobe -r only removes it from the running kernel for now.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between changing a kernel module or parameter for the running system and making that change permanent, and name one risk or tradeoff of tuning these at runtime.
lessons.modelAnswer: Kernel modules are loadable chunks of kernel code, mostly drivers. I check what is loaded with lsmod, inspect one with modinfo, and load or remove it with modprobe, which pulls in dependencies for me, unlike insmod. Kernel parameters are tunable values exposed under /proc/sys, and sysctl reads or sets them, for example sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1. Both kinds of change act on the live kernel only, so they vanish at reboot. To make them stick, I put parameters in a file in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply with sysctl --system, list modules to load in /etc/modules-load.d/, and blacklist unwanted ones in /etc/modprobe.d/. The tradeoff is that runtime changes are instant and easy to test, but if you forget to persist them the system drifts back after a reboot, and a wrong value applied live can break networking or stability immediately.
rubricPoints: Defines a kernel module as loadable kernel code such as a driver.
Names lsmod, modinfo and modprobe and notes modprobe handles dependencies.
Explains kernel parameters live under /proc/sys and are managed with sysctl.
States that runtime changes are lost at reboot unless saved to config files.
Names the persistence locations such as /etc/sysctl.d, /etc/modules-load.d or /etc/modprobe.d.
Identifies a risk, such as forgotten persistence or a bad live value breaking the system.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner load modules or tune sysctl values, so careful reading of the commands and the runtime-versus-persistent distinction is the best fit for now.

lessons.plain: Linux decides who may do what by asking three questions: who are you (your user account), which teams are you on (your groups), and what do the rules on this file allow for someone like you (its permissions). Think of an office building: every person has a badge, badges belong to departments, and each room has a sign saying what the room owner, members of one department, and everyone else may do inside. Managing users, groups, and permissions means creating those badges, assigning departments, and writing the signs so people and programs can do their work without getting into rooms they should not.
lessons.guessPrompt: A file's permissions show as rw-r----- and it belongs to user root and group app. A user named deploy is not root and is not in the app group. Can deploy read the file, and what is one way you could let deploy read it without letting everyone read it?
lessons.teach:
A user is an account identified by a number called a UID (user ID); root is UID 0 and can override permissions. A group is a named set of users identified by a GID (group ID). Accounts are listed in /etc/passwd, password hashes live in /etc/shadow (readable only by root), and group membership is in /etc/group. You create users with useradd, change them with usermod, create groups with groupadd, and check someone's identity with id.

Every file has one owner user, one owner group, and three sets of permission bits: for the owner, for the group, and for others (everyone else). Each set holds r (read), w (write), and x (execute, or enter for a directory). Linux checks only the first set that applies to you, which is why it is predictable. Bits are often written as octal digits: r=4, w=2, x=1, so 640 means owner rw, group r, others nothing. chmod changes the bits; chown changes the owner and group.

Worked example: ls -l shows a config file as -rw-r----- root app. Step one, id deploy shows deploy is not in app, so deploy falls into others and gets nothing. Step two, run usermod -aG app deploy to append deploy to the app group. Step three, deploy must start a new login session, because group membership is read at login. Step four, deploy now matches the group set and can read but not change the file.

A common mistake is running usermod -G app deploy without -a. That replaces all of deploy's extra groups with just app, silently removing access elsewhere. Another is reaching for chmod 777, which grants everyone full access and hides the real problem.

In a running system, a service runs as its own user; if that user cannot read its config or write its log directory, the service fails to start, so fixing ownership or group membership is usually the correct repair rather than loosening permissions for everyone.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, ls -l shows the file /data/rx.csv as -rw----r-- pharm audit, which is mode 604. The user tom is a member of the audit group. Step 1: decode 604. Owner 6 = rw, group 0 = nothing, others 4 = r. Step 2: tom is not the user pharm, so the owner set does not apply to him. Step 3: ______. Step 4: tom cannot read the file, even though a user who is outside the audit group can read it. Which statement is the missing Step 3?
choices: Because the group set grants nothing, Linux moves on to the others set and gives tom r.
Others means everyone on the system, so tom receives r like every other account.
tom is in audit, so the group set is the first set that applies to him. Linux stops there and gives him nothing.
Linux adds the group and others sets together, so tom gets r from the others set.
questions.why: Linux checks only the first permission set that matches you, and for a member of the file's group that set is the group set, which here is 0, so tom gets no access.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's script must give its owner read, write and execute, give its group read and execute, and give others no access. Using r=4, w=2 and x=1, which octal mode should be passed to chmod?
questions.why: The owner gets 4+2+1=7, the group gets 4+1=5 and others get 0, which makes 750. Mode 755 would wrongly give others read and execute.

questions.prompt: The user kai belongs to the extra groups docker and wheel. An admin wants kai to also join the backup group and runs usermod -G backup kai, without the -a option. What happens?
choices: kai's extra groups are replaced by backup alone, so kai loses docker and wheel.
kai keeps docker and wheel and is also added to backup.
The command fails because -a is required whenever -G is used.
kai is added to backup, but only for the current login session.
questions.why: Without -a (append), usermod -G replaces the whole list of extra groups. kai silently loses docker and wheel and keeps only backup.

questions.prompt: An online shop's web service runs as its own user, webapp. It fails to start because it cannot write to its log directory, /var/log/shopsite. ls -l shows the directory as drwxr-xr-x root root (mode 755). What is the most appropriate repair?
choices: Make webapp the owner of the directory with chown, so the owner set (rwx) applies to the service.
Change the directory to mode 744 so the others set gets fewer rights.
Add webapp to the root group with usermod -aG root webapp.
Run chmod 777 on the directory so the service can write to it.
questions.why: After chown, webapp matches the owner set, which already includes w. That fixes the real problem without loosening access for everyone. The group set (r-x) has no write bit, so joining the root group would not help, and 777 opens the directory to all users.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Linux decides whether a user can read a file, using owner, group, and others, and describe the tradeoff between fixing an access problem with group membership versus with chmod.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every file has an owner user, an owner group, and three permission sets: owner, group, and others, each with read, write, and execute. Linux checks which set applies to you, owner first, then group, then others, and uses only that one. Root can bypass this. So if a service user can't read a config file, I check ls -l for the owner, group, and bits, and id for the user's groups. The clean fix is usually adding the user to the file's group with usermod -aG, remembering the -a so existing groups aren't wiped and that a new login is needed. That grants access only to that user. Using chmod to open the file to others is faster but gives every account on the machine access, which can expose secrets. The tradeoff is precision and safety versus speed.
rubricPoints: Names the three permission classes: owner, group, others.
States that only the first matching class is applied and root can bypass checks.
Mentions checking with ls -l and id before changing anything.
Uses usermod -aG and warns that omitting -a replaces existing groups.
Notes group changes apply after a new login.
Explains that loosening with chmod for others exposes the file to every account.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose and repair a real permission problem blocking a service, which is exactly this objective in practice.

lessons.plain: Every person or program that uses a Linux server needs an account, called a user. Users can be gathered into groups, which are named collections of users that share access to the same files and tools. Think of an office building. Each employee gets their own badge, which is the user. Badges can also be tagged with team names, which are the groups, and a door can open for everyone on a team. Managing users and groups means creating badges, adding or removing team tags, and checking who belongs where. Done well, people can reach exactly what their job needs and nothing more.
lessons.guessPrompt: Maria is already in the 'developers' group. An admin runs a command meant to put her in the 'docker' group too, but afterwards she can no longer reach developer files. What do you think the command did to her group list?
lessons.teach:
A user is an account with a name and a numeric user ID (UID). Linux records users in /etc/passwd, a text file listing each account's name, UID, home directory and login shell. A login shell is the program that reads your commands. Hashed passwords live separately in /etc/shadow, a file only root can read. Root is the all-powerful administrator account.

A group is a named set of users with a numeric group ID (GID), recorded in /etc/group. Each user has exactly one primary group, which new files they create belong to by default. A user can also have any number of supplementary groups, which are extra memberships that grant shared access. Access checks compare the IDs on a file with your UID and all of your GIDs, so adding someone to a group grants that group's access at once.

Three commands handle most of the work. useradd creates an account: -m makes a home directory, -s sets the login shell, -G lists supplementary groups. usermod changes an existing account. groups shows which groups a user belongs to. You create a new group with groupadd and set a password with passwd.

Worked example. First, groupadd webteam creates the group. Second, useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G webteam ana creates ana with a home directory, the bash shell and webteam membership. Third, passwd ana sets her password. Fourth, usermod -aG docker ana adds docker while keeping webteam. Finally, groups ana now lists ana (her primary group, often created with the same name), webteam and docker.

The classic mistake is running usermod -G docker ana without -a. The -a flag means append. Without it, the list you give replaces all of her supplementary groups, so she silently loses webteam. On a running server, that can lock a user out of shared project files or deployment tools. A second gotcha is timing: group changes only apply to new login sessions, so the user must log out and back in before the new access works.

questions.prompt: At a small dental clinic, the server already has a user named lin whose supplementary groups are lin's existing membership in records. The office manager wants lin to also join a new group called billing without losing access to records. The admin works through it like this. Step 1: groupadd billing creates the new group. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: groups lin now lists lin, records and billing. Step 4: lin logs out and logs back in so the new membership takes effect. Which command belongs in Step 2?
choices: usermod -G billing lin
usermod -aG billing lin
useradd -G billing lin
groupadd -G billing lin
questions.why: usermod changes an existing account, and -a appends billing to her supplementary groups so records is kept, which matches the output in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A user named tomas has the primary group tomas and the supplementary groups audio and devs. When tomas creates a new file, which group does that file belong to by default?
choices: tomas, because new files belong to the primary group
audio, because supplementary groups are checked first
No group at all until root assigns one
devs, because it is the most recently added group
questions.why: Each user has exactly one primary group, and new files the user creates belong to that group by default; supplementary groups only add extra shared access.

questions.prompt: At a game studio, an admin needs to create a brand-new account called ravi with a home directory, the login shell /bin/zsh, and membership in the existing supplementary group qa. Which single command does this?
choices: useradd -s /bin/zsh -G qa ravi
groupadd -m -s /bin/zsh -G qa ravi
useradd -m -s /bin/zsh -G qa ravi
usermod -m -s /bin/zsh -aG qa ravi
questions.why: useradd creates a new account, -m makes the home directory, -s sets the login shell and -G lists the supplementary groups.

questions.prompt: On a university research server, an admin runs usermod -aG gpuusers mei, and groups mei correctly shows gpuusers. Mei is still logged in from earlier in the day, and her attempt to open a file owned by gpuusers is denied. What is the most likely reason?
choices: gpuusers must be made her primary group before it grants access
The -a flag removed her other supplementary groups
Group changes only apply to new login sessions, so she must log out and back in
Group memberships are stored in /etc/shadow, which she cannot read
questions.why: A new group membership is only picked up when the user starts a new login session, so her existing session still runs with her old set of groups.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give an existing user access to a new group without breaking their current access, and name one limit or pitfall of how group changes take effect.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every account has a UID and one primary group, plus optional supplementary groups that grant shared access. The system stores users in /etc/passwd and groups in /etc/group. To add an existing user to another group, I run usermod -aG newgroup username. The -a is essential, because it appends the group. Plain -G replaces every supplementary group the user already has, which could quietly cut them off from project files. Afterwards I run groups username to confirm the old groups are still there and the new one appears. One pitfall is that the change does not reach sessions that are already open. The user has to log out and back in before the new permission works, so 'I added you and it still fails' usually just means a stale session. The tradeoff is that groups are coarse: everyone in the group gets the same access.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the primary group from supplementary groups.
Uses usermod -aG and explains that -a appends rather than replaces.
Verifies the result with the groups command.
Notes that group changes apply only after a new login.
Mentions where users and groups are stored, /etc/passwd and /etc/group.

suggested.rationale: No current mission has the learner create accounts, so reasoning through an exam-style multi-user scenario best tests choosing the right flags, such as -aG versus -G.

lessons.plain: Every file on a Linux system has an owner (one user), a group (a named set of users), and three sets of permissions: one for the owner, one for the group, and one for everyone else. Each set says whether that audience may read (r), write (w), or execute (x) the file. Think of an office filing cabinet with three keys: one for the person whose name is on the drawer, one for their team, and one for visitors. chmod changes which keys open what, chown changes whose name is on the drawer, and umask sets which keys new drawers start without.
lessons.guessPrompt: A config file is owned by user alice, belongs to the group web, and only alice may read it. A web service running as a different user in the web group cannot start. What single change would you guess lets the service read the file without letting every user on the server read it?
lessons.teach:
Linux permissions decide who may do what to a file or directory. Each file has an owner (a user account), a group (a named collection of accounts), and three permission triplets: owner, group, and others (everyone else). Each triplet holds r (read), w (write) and x (execute). On a directory, r lets you list names, w lets you create or delete entries, and x lets you enter the directory and reach files inside it. The system checks only one triplet: owner if you own the file, otherwise group if you are a member, otherwise others.

Permissions are often written as octal digits, where r=4, w=2, x=1, added together. So rwx is 7, rw- is 6, r-x is 5, r-- is 4. The mode 640 means owner rw-, group r--, others ---.

chmod changes the mode, either numerically (chmod 640 app.conf) or symbolically (chmod g+r app.conf adds group read). chown changes ownership: chown alice:web app.conf sets owner alice and group web. Changing ownership normally needs root.

umask is a per-process mask of permissions to remove from new files and directories. New files start from 666 and new directories from 777, then the umask bits are taken away. Worked example with umask 022: a new file is 666 minus write for group and others, giving 644 (rw-r--r--). A new directory is 777 minus the same bits, giving 755 (rwxr-xr-x). With umask 027, files become 640 and directories 750, so others get nothing.

A common mistake is fixing an access error with chmod 777. It works, but it lets every user, and any compromised process, change or replace the file. Another mistake is forgetting x on a parent directory: the file itself may be readable, yet nobody in that group can reach it. On a running server, wrong permissions on a config or key file usually show up as a service that fails to start with a permission denied error, while overly loose ones become a quiet security hole.

questions.prompt:
A small accounting firm runs its nightly backup job with umask 007. The admin works out what permissions the job's new items will get.

Step 1: A new file starts from 666 (rw-rw-rw-).
Step 2: The umask 007 removes read, write and execute for others, so the file becomes 660 (rw-rw----).
Step 3: A new directory starts from 777 (rwxrwxrwx).
Step 4: ???

What is the correct Step 4?
choices: The umask value becomes the mode, so the directory becomes 007 (------rwx).
The umask removes write for group and others, so the directory becomes 750 (rwxr-x---).
The umask removes the same bits from the file's result, so the directory becomes 660 (rw-rw----).
The umask removes everything for others, so the directory becomes 770 (rwxrwx---).
questions.why: A directory starts from 777, and removing the 007 bits takes away only the others triplet, which leaves 770 (rwxrwx---).

questions.prompt: A script on a web host has mode 754. What does each class of user get?
choices: Owner r-x, group r--, others rwx
Owner rwx, group r-x, others r--
Owner rw-, group r-x, others r--
Owner rwx, group rw-, others r-x
questions.why: Each digit is a sum of r=4, w=2, x=1, so 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x (4+1) and 4 is r--.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, the file /srv/ledger/report.csv has mode 640 and is owned by root:finance. The directory /srv/ledger has mode 760 and is owned by root:finance. Priya is in the finance group, but she gets permission denied when she opens the report. Which change fixes this with the least extra access?
choices: chmod o+r /srv/ledger/report.csv
chown priya:priya /srv/ledger
chmod g+x /srv/ledger
chmod 777 /srv/ledger/report.csv
questions.why: The group triplet on the directory is rw- (6), and it lacks x, so group members cannot enter the directory to reach the file. Adding group execute lets them in without opening anything to other users.

questions.prompt: A file at a design studio is owned by eve, its group is ops, and its mode is 460 (r--rw----). Eve is a member of ops. She tries to save a change to the file. What happens?
choices: She is denied, because she is the owner, so only the owner triplet r-- is checked.
She succeeds, because her ops membership gives her the group triplet rw-.
She succeeds, because Linux combines the owner and group triplets and grants the most access.
She is denied, because the others triplet is ---, and others is always checked last.
questions.why: Linux checks only one triplet. Eve owns the file, so only the owner bits r-- apply, and the group's rw- is ignored for her.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let a service account read a config file that currently only its owner can read, covering owner, group and others, the commands you would use, and why chmod 777 is the wrong shortcut.
lessons.modelAnswer: Linux checks exactly one of three permission sets: owner if you own the file, group if you belong to its group, otherwise others. Each set has read, write and execute, which in octal are 4, 2 and 1. Our config is 600, so only the owner can read it. I would put the file in a group the service account belongs to with chown alice:web app.conf, then add group read with chmod 640 app.conf. The owner keeps read and write, the group can only read, and others get nothing. I would also check the parent directories give the group x, or it still cannot reach the file. chmod 777 would also make the error go away, but it lets every account change the file, which is a security tradeoff we should not accept. Finally, umask controls defaults for new files, so a umask of 027 keeps future files closed to others.
rubricPoints: Names the three audiences owner, group and others and says only one set is checked.
Maps r, w, x to 4, 2, 1 and reads a mode like 640 correctly.
Uses chown to set owner and group and chmod to set the mode.
Explains umask removes bits from the 666 file and 777 directory defaults.
Rejects chmod 777 because it grants write to everyone.
Mentions directory execute permission is needed to reach files inside.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose and fix a real permission problem on a service, which directly exercises reading modes, chmod and chown.

lessons.plain: Normal Linux permissions say who may read, change, or run a file. Special permissions are three extra switches that change how that access behaves. SUID lets a program run with the power of the file's owner instead of the person who launched it. SGID does the same for the file's group, and on a folder it makes new files join the folder's group automatically. The sticky bit, on a shared folder, means you can only delete your own files. Think of an office supply room. SUID is a staff badge lent to a visitor for one errand. SGID is a team label on the door. The sticky bit means nobody may throw out anyone else's box.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a shared scratch folder where every user is allowed to create files. What rule would you want so that one user cannot delete or rename another user's files there?
lessons.teach:
Special permissions are three extra bits that sit alongside the normal read, write and execute bits. They change how a program runs or how a directory behaves.

SUID (set user ID) goes on an executable program. It makes the program run with the identity of the file's owner, not the identity of whoever started it. The password-changing program is the classic case. It is owned by root, the all-powerful administrator account, so ordinary users can update the protected password file through it.

SGID (set group ID) on a program runs it with the file's group. On a directory, it makes new files inside inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's own primary group.

The sticky bit on a directory means only a file's owner, the directory's owner, or root may delete or rename files there. This holds even when everyone can write to the directory.

In octal (numeric) mode, these bits form an extra leading digit: SUID is 4, SGID is 2, sticky is 1, and you add them together. In a long listing they replace an execute letter. You see s in the owner slot for SUID, s in the group slot for SGID, and t in the others slot for sticky. A capital S or T means the bit is set but execute is missing, which usually signals a mistake.

Worked example: a team shares /srv/project. Step 1: give the directory the group devs. Step 2: run chmod 2775 /srv/project. The 2 adds SGID, and 775 gives owner and group full access. Step 3: alice creates notes.txt. It belongs to group devs, so bob can edit it. Using 3775 instead also adds the sticky bit, so bob cannot delete alice's file. The shared /tmp directory is typically 1777.

Common mistake: putting SUID on a root-owned program to fix an access problem. Every user who runs it gains root's power, so one flaw in that program means full system takeover. In a running system, unexpected SUID-root files are a classic sign of compromise, which is why administrators audit for them.

questions.prompt: A design agency keeps shared artwork in /data/campaigns, which belongs to the group artists. The lead wants three things. First, new files should automatically belong to artists. Second, artists must not be able to delete or rename each other's files. Third, the owner and group get full access and others get nothing. Worked so far: the owner and group need read, write and execute, which is 7 and 7. Others get no access, which is 0. So the normal part is 770. Missing step: work out the extra leading digit. Inheriting the directory's group needs one special bit, and protecting files from deletion by other users needs another. Add their values. Final command: chmod ____ /data/campaigns. Which value completes the command?
questions.why: SGID (2) makes new files inherit the group, and the sticky bit (1) restricts deletion to owners; 2 + 1 = 3, which gives 3770.

questions.prompt: On a server at a shipping company, a long listing of /usr/local/bin/labelprint shows -rwsr-xr-x, and the owner is root. A warehouse clerk with an ordinary account runs it. Whose identity does the program run with?
choices: Nobody's identity, because the s means execute has been disabled
The clerk's own identity, because the clerk started the program
Root's identity, because the s in the owner slot means SUID is set
The file's group identity, because an s always means SGID
questions.why: An s in the owner execute slot means SUID is set, so the program runs as the file's owner (root), not as the person who started it.

questions.prompt: A university lab admin checks a shared upload directory, and the listing shows drwxrwxrwT. What does the capital T most likely tell the admin?
choices: SUID is set on the directory, so files run as the directory's owner
SGID is set, so new files inherit the directory's group
The sticky bit is set and others have full execute access, which is the ideal setup
The sticky bit is set but execute is missing for others, which usually signals a mistake
questions.why: A capital T in the others slot means the sticky bit is on but the execute permission underneath is missing, which is usually an error.

questions.prompt: During a routine check at a hospital, an administrator finds a program in an ordinary user's home folder. The program is owned by root and has SUID set, and nobody remembers installing it. What is the best interpretation?
choices: It is harmless, because SUID only matters on directories
It only lets users delete each other's files, so it is a minor nuisance
It is normal, because every program in a home folder gets SUID by default
It is a warning sign of possible compromise, because anyone running it gains root's power
questions.why: An unexpected SUID-root program gives root's power to anyone who runs it, which is why such files are a classic sign of compromise that administrators audit for.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the shared project folder uses mode 2775 and /tmp uses 1777, and whether you could just put SUID on a tool to let everyone use it. Explain SUID, SGID and the sticky bit in your own words, including the security tradeoff of SUID.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each of these is an extra permission bit on top of rwx. SUID, value 4, makes a program run as its file owner. That is how an ordinary user can change their password through a root-owned program. The tradeoff is risk: a SUID-root program hands root power to anyone who runs it, so any bug becomes a full compromise. It is not a casual fix, and stray SUID files should be audited. SGID, value 2, on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group. That is why our project folder is 2775: everyone's files land in the team group and stay editable by the team. The sticky bit, value 1, on a directory means only a file's owner, the directory owner, or root can delete or rename files there. /tmp is 1777 so anyone can write, but nobody can remove other people's files. In ls, these show as s, s and t, and a capital letter means execute is missing.
rubricPoints: SUID makes a program run with the file owner's identity, not the caller's.
SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, which suits shared team folders.
The sticky bit on a writable directory limits deletion and renaming to the file owner, the directory owner, or root.
The octal values are 4, 2 and 1 in a leading digit, shown as s, s and t in a listing.
SUID-root programs are a security risk and should be minimized and audited.

suggested.rationale: No current mission sets special bits directly, so reasoning through an exam-style shared-server scenario is the best way to practice choosing between SUID, SGID and the sticky bit and decoding modes like 2775 and 1777.

lessons.plain: A network service is a program that runs quietly in the background on a server and waits for other computers to ask it for something. Linux calls these background programs daemons. Each one listens on a numbered door called a port. Four common ones: SSH lets you log in and run commands remotely over an encrypted connection. A web server hands out web pages. A print server accepts print jobs from many machines and queues them for a shared printer. A time service keeps the server's clock matched to trusted clocks on the network. Think of a hotel front desk with separate windows for keys, mail and wake-up calls.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a server's clock drifts five minutes away from the real time, what kinds of problems do you think people running it might notice?
lessons.teach:
A network service is a daemon (a background program) that listens on a port, a numbered endpoint on the machine, and answers requests from other computers. On modern Linux, systemd (the program that starts and supervises services) controls daemons through the systemctl command. systemctl start runs a service now. systemctl enable makes it start at every boot. systemctl status shows whether it is running. The ss -tlnp command lists which ports are listening and which program owns each one.

SSH (Secure Shell) gives you an encrypted remote login. Its daemon is sshd, it listens on port 22, and its server settings live in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Web servers such as Apache (httpd or apache2) and nginx serve pages on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS, which is HTTP encrypted with a certificate. Printing is usually handled by CUPS (Common Unix Printing System), which queues jobs and listens on port 631. Time synchronization uses NTP (Network Time Protocol) on UDP port 123. On current distributions the NTP client is usually chronyd (checked with chronyc sources), and the older one is ntpd. timedatectl shows whether the clock is synchronized.

Worked example, hardening SSH on a new server. First, systemctl status sshd confirms the daemon is running. Second, ss -tlnp shows sshd listening on port 22. Third, you edit sshd_config and set PermitRootLogin no, so nobody can log in directly as the all-powerful root account. Fourth, you keep your current session open and run systemctl restart sshd so the daemon rereads its file. Fifth, you open a second login to prove you can still get in before you close the first one.

A common mistake is running start without enable. The service works today, then silently disappears after the next reboot. Another is editing a config file and never restarting or reloading, so the old settings stay in force. Clocks matter too. If NTP is not working, timestamps in logs from different servers stop lining up, and encrypted connections and logins that check certificate dates or ticket times can fail.

questions.prompt: A small bakery chain is setting up a new Linux server to host its online ordering site with the nginx web server. The admin traces these steps. Step 1: run systemctl start nginx so the web server runs right now. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: run ss -tlnp and see nginx listening on ports 80 and 443. Step 4: reboot the server, then run systemctl status nginx and confirm nginx came back up on its own without anyone starting it by hand. Which command belongs in Step 2 so that Step 4 succeeds?
choices: systemctl restart nginx, so the daemon rereads its configuration file
systemctl enable nginx, so systemd starts the service at every boot
chronyc sources, so the server clock is correct before the reboot
systemctl status nginx, to record that the service is currently running
questions.why: start only runs the service now. enable is what makes systemd launch nginx at every boot, so it is back after the reboot in Step 4.

questions.prompt: At a regional library, an admin compares log files from two Linux servers while investigating a failed login. The timestamps for the same event differ by about six minutes between the machines. Which command should the admin run first on each server to see whether its clock is being synchronized?
choices: ss -tlnp
systemctl enable sshd
timedatectl
systemctl status cups
questions.why: timedatectl shows whether the clock is synchronized. Log timestamps that do not line up across servers are a classic sign that time sync (NTP) is not working.

questions.prompt: An admin at a design studio edits the configuration file of the company's Apache web server to change a setting. The service shows as running in systemctl status, but the website still behaves exactly as it did before the edit. No errors were reported. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The daemon was never restarted or reloaded, so the old settings are still in force
The service was started but never enabled, so it ignores configuration changes
The web server is listening on port 631 instead of port 80
The NTP client is not running, so the file's timestamp is wrong
questions.why: A daemon keeps using the settings it loaded when it started. Until it is restarted or reloaded, the edited file has no effect.

questions.prompt: A secondary school's IT team is writing firewall rules for one Linux server. Students must reach the school's encrypted (HTTPS) web pages, and staff must send jobs to the CUPS print service on the same machine. Which two ports must be allowed?
choices: 443 for HTTPS and 631 for CUPS
22 for HTTPS and 631 for CUPS
443 for HTTPS and 123 for CUPS
80 for HTTPS and 631 for CUPS
questions.why: HTTPS, which is HTTP encrypted with a certificate, uses port 443. CUPS listens on port 631. Port 80 is plain HTTP, 123 is NTP, and 22 is SSH.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a network service is on Linux, using SSH, a web server, CUPS and NTP as examples, and name one tradeoff or limit you must keep in mind when running them.
lessons.modelAnswer: A network service is a daemon, a background program that listens on a port and answers requests. systemd manages them. We start one with systemctl start, make it survive reboots with systemctl enable, and check listening ports with ss -tlnp. sshd gives encrypted remote shells on port 22. Apache or nginx serve web pages on 80 and 443. CUPS queues print jobs on 631. chronyd or ntpd keep the clock in sync over UDP 123. The tradeoff is that every listening service is another door an attacker can try, so we only run what we need and harden what we keep, for example by turning off root login over SSH. Two limits to remember: changes to a config file do nothing until the service is restarted or reloaded. And if time sync fails, logs from different servers stop lining up and logins that check timestamps can fail.
rubricPoints: Defines a service as a background daemon listening on a port.
Names each service with its role and default port: SSH 22, web 80/443, CUPS 631, NTP 123.
Distinguishes systemctl start from enable and notes that config changes need a restart or reload.
Names a tradeoff, such as each open service adding attack surface or the need for hardening.
Explains why accurate time matters for logs and authentication.

suggested.rationale: Investigating failed SSH logins has the learner work with a real sshd service and its logs, which turns the port, daemon and hardening ideas into practice.

lessons.plain: An environment variable is a named value, like HOME or PATH, that a running program can look up to learn about its surroundings: who the user is, where to find commands, which editor to open. Think of it as a sticky note handed to each new program when it starts. Each child program gets a copy of the parent's notes, not the original.
