Shell configuration files are small text files the shell (the command interpreter you type into) reads when it starts. Putting settings in these files is how they come back every time you log in.
lessons.guessPrompt: You type MYAPP=prod in a terminal, then run a script that prints MYAPP, and the script prints nothing. Why might the script not see the value you just set?
lessons.teach:
An environment variable is a name=value pair that a process (a running program) passes down to every child process it starts. A shell variable is one that lives only inside the current shell. The export command turns a shell variable into an environment variable so children inherit it. Inheritance runs one way: a child gets a copy at startup, and nothing a child changes flows back to its parent. Useful commands: env or printenv lists the environment, echo $NAME shows one value, and unset NAME removes it. Key variables include PATH (the colon-separated list of directories searched for commands), HOME (your home directory), USER, SHELL, and EDITOR.

Settings vanish when the shell exits, so we put them in startup files. Bash, the common shell, reads different files depending on how it starts. A login shell, such as an SSH session or console login, reads /etc/profile (system-wide, which usually also pulls in scripts in /etc/profile.d/), then the first one it finds of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile. An interactive non-login shell, such as a new terminal window inside a desktop, reads ~/.bashrc, plus a system-wide file named /etc/bashrc or /etc/bash.bashrc depending on the distribution. Many ~/.bash_profile files contain a line that loads ~/.bashrc, so login shells get both. The command source file (or a single dot, . file) re-reads a file in the current shell without logging out.

Worked example: you add export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools/bin to ~/.bashrc. First, in your already-open session, the tool is still not found, because the file was only read at startup. Second, you run source ~/.bashrc, and PATH now ends with /opt/tools/bin. Third, you SSH in fresh, and it works because ~/.bash_profile loads ~/.bashrc.

Common mistake: setting MYAPP=prod without export, so child scripts never see it. In a running system, remember that services started by systemd and jobs started by cron do not read your shell files at all, so a variable that works in your terminal can be missing for the service.

questions.prompt: Priya manages the ordering server at a small bakery. Her backup script, run from her shell, should read a variable called REPORT_DIR. Step 1: At the prompt she types REPORT_DIR=/srv/reports and then runs ./backup.sh. The script prints an empty value for REPORT_DIR. Step 2: (missing) Step 3: She runs ./backup.sh again, and this time it prints /srv/reports. Step 4: So the setting survives logging out, she adds the line export REPORT_DIR=/srv/reports to her ~/.bash_profile. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: She runs export REPORT_DIR so child processes inherit the variable.
She runs echo $REPORT_DIR to confirm the value is stored in the shell.
She runs source ~/.bashrc so the shell re-reads its startup file.
She edits backup.sh so the script sets REPORT_DIR and passes it back to the shell.
questions.why: REPORT_DIR began as a shell variable that only the current shell could see, and export turns it into an environment variable, so the script, a child process, gets a copy when it starts.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, Tomas runs a script from his Bash prompt. Inside the script is the line export WAREHOUSE=north. The script finishes, and Tomas types echo $WAREHOUSE at the same prompt. What does he see, and why?
choices: north, because export makes a variable visible to every process on the system, including the parent shell.
An error, because export can only be used in startup files such as ~/.bash_profile.
north, because a script always runs inside the same process as the shell that started it.
Nothing. The script ran as a child process, and changes made in a child never flow back to its parent shell.
questions.why: Inheritance only goes from parent to child, so the parent shell never receives the variable that the child script exported.

questions.prompt: A new admin at a museum adds export EDITOR=vim to ~/.bash_profile. Their ~/.bashrc does not mention it. Later, while working in a graphical desktop, they open a new terminal window and run echo $EDITOR, and the output is empty. What explains this?
choices: EDITOR is a shell variable, and Bash refuses to export shell variables.
The new terminal is a login shell, and login shells read only /etc/profile.
The new terminal is an interactive non-login shell, so it reads ~/.bashrc instead of ~/.bash_profile.
~/.bash_profile is read only by root, so ordinary users never get its settings.
questions.why: A new terminal window inside a desktop starts an interactive non-login shell, and that kind of shell reads ~/.bashrc, not ~/.bash_profile.

questions.prompt: At a ticketing startup, the setting API_MODE=live is exported in a developer's ~/.bashrc. When the developer runs the app from their terminal, it works. When the same app runs as a service started by systemd, API_MODE is missing. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Services started by systemd do not read a user's shell startup files at all.
systemd only reads environment variables whose names appear in the PATH list.
The developer forgot to run source ~/.bashrc before starting systemd.
Variables in ~/.bashrc must be removed with unset before systemd can read them.
questions.why: systemd starts services without going through the user's Bash startup files, so a variable that a shell file provides is never set for the service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a variable they added to their ~/.bashrc works in their terminal but not for everyone, or not in a cron job, and which file they would use instead. Name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: An environment variable is a name=value pair that a process copies to the programs it starts. You need export, or children won't see it, and changes never flow back up to the parent. ~/.bashrc is read by your own interactive non-login shells, and usually by login shells too, because ~/.bash_profile loads it. So it only affects you, and only shells started after you edited it or ran source. For every user's login shell, put it in /etc/profile or a script in /etc/profile.d/. The limit is that cron and systemd services don't start a login or interactive shell, so they read none of these files. For those, set the variable in the job or service definition itself. The tradeoff is that system-wide files affect everyone, so a mistake there breaks every login, while per-user files are safer but narrower.
rubricPoints: Defines an environment variable as a name=value pair inherited by child processes, and says export is needed.
Notes that inheritance is a one-way copy from parent to child.
Distinguishes per-user files (~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile) from system-wide ones (/etc/profile, /etc/profile.d/).
Explains login versus interactive non-login shells and which files each reads.
Mentions source, or a new shell, to apply changes.
Notes that cron and services do not read shell startup files.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through scenarios about which startup file a given kind of shell reads and whether a variable is inherited, and no current mission or planned engine drills this directly.

lessons.plain: Print and email services on Linux both work like a post office sorting room. When you print, you do not talk to the printer directly. You hand your document to a print service, which lines jobs up in a queue and feeds them to the printer one at a time. On Linux that service is usually CUPS. Email works similarly. A program called a mail transfer agent accepts a message, holds it in a waiting line, and passes it hop by hop toward the recipient's server. In both cases a background service stores work safely and delivers it later, so a busy printer or an unreachable server does not lose your job.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you send three documents to a printer that is switched off, what do you think happens to them, and why might that be better than an error message?
lessons.teach:
CUPS (Common Unix Printing System) is the standard Linux print service. It runs as a background process, called a daemon, named cupsd. It manages print queues. A print queue is a named waiting line tied to one printer, and jobs are stored on disk in a spool directory until the printer takes them. CUPS speaks IPP (Internet Printing Protocol) on port 631 and offers a web admin page there. Common commands are lp or lpr to submit a job, lpstat to show queues and jobs, cancel or lprm to remove a job, and lpadmin to add or configure printers.

A mail transfer agent (MTA) is a server program that moves email between machines using SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), normally on port 25. Postfix, Sendmail and Exim are common MTAs. It works alongside two other roles. The MUA (mail user agent) is the program a person reads and writes mail in. The MDA (mail delivery agent) drops a message into a user's mailbox, often under /var/spool/mail or /var/mail. An MTA keeps undeliverable mail in a mail queue and retries later. You can view that queue with mailq. The aliases file maps names like root to real users, and you rebuild it with newaliases.

Here is a worked example. A cron job on a server emails root. First, the local MTA accepts the message. Second, it checks the aliases file and finds that root maps to alice. Third, alice's mailbox is on this machine, so the MDA writes the message to her mailbox. If the mail were addressed to another domain, the MTA would look up that domain's mail server and connect over SMTP. If that server was down, the message would wait in the mailq and be retried.

A common mistake is configuring an MTA to accept and forward mail from anyone on the internet. That is called an open relay. Spammers find open relays quickly, so the server's address gets blocklisted, and its legitimate mail starts bouncing. Restrict relaying to trusted networks or authenticated users.

questions.prompt: At a small bakery's office, Raj needs to print invoice.pdf on the printer whose print queue is named front-desk. Step 1: Raj runs lp -d front-desk invoice.pdf, and the CUPS daemon (cupsd) accepts the job. Step 2: The printer is out of paper, so the job is held on disk in the spool directory. Step 3 (missing): Raj wants to see whether his job is still waiting in the front-desk queue and what its job ID is. Step 4: He sees the job listed as front-desk-42 and removes it with cancel front-desk-42. Which command fills Step 3?
choices: lpadmin, to open the front-desk printer's settings
newaliases, to refresh the list of known queue names
mailq, to list the jobs that are waiting to be sent
lpstat, to show the print queues and the jobs in them
questions.why: lpstat shows CUPS print queues and their waiting jobs, while mailq shows the mail queue, lpadmin adds or configures printers, and newaliases rebuilds the mail aliases file.

questions.prompt: On a Linux mail server, which program's job is to drop an arriving message into a user's mailbox, for example a file under /var/mail?
choices: The mail delivery agent (MDA)
The print daemon cupsd
The aliases file
The mail user agent (MUA)
questions.why: The MDA does the final step of writing a message into the user's mailbox, while the MUA is the program a person reads and writes mail in.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's server runs Postfix, a mail transfer agent. It tries to send a report to a partner company at another domain, but the partner's mail server is offline for maintenance. What should the administrator expect, and how can they check?
choices: The message is rebuilt into the aliases file, and newaliases sends it again
The message waits in the mail queue to be retried later, and mailq shows it
The message is written into root's local mailbox instead, and lpstat lists it
The message is dropped right away, and the CUPS web page on port 631 shows the error
questions.why: An MTA keeps undeliverable mail in its mail queue and retries it later, and mailq displays that queue.

questions.prompt: A design studio set up its mail transfer agent to accept and forward mail from any computer on the internet. A few weeks later, the studio's ordinary business emails start bouncing. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?
choices: The mail queue is full; run mailq to clear it, and leave relaying settings unchanged
The server became an open relay, spammers used it and its address was blocklisted; restrict relaying to trusted networks or authenticated users
The aliases file is outdated; run newaliases, and keep accepting mail from anyone
Port 25 is reserved for printing; move SMTP to port 631
questions.why: Accepting and forwarding mail from anyone makes an open relay, which spammers abuse until the server is blocklisted, so relaying must be limited to trusted networks or authenticated users.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a print job and an email each travel from a user to their destination on a Linux server, naming the roles involved and one risk or tradeoff of running these services.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both services hand work to a background daemon that queues it on disk, so nothing is lost if the destination is busy. For printing, a user runs lp or lpr. CUPS, whose daemon is cupsd, puts the job in the named print queue in its spool directory and sends it to the printer over IPP on port 631. lpstat shows the queue and cancel removes a job. For email, the user writes the message in a mail user agent. A mail transfer agent such as Postfix relays it over SMTP on port 25. A mail delivery agent then drops it into the recipient's mailbox. Failed deliveries sit in the mail queue, which mailq shows, and get retried. The tradeoff is exposure. A listening service is an attack surface, and an MTA that relays for anyone becomes an open relay that gets the server blocklisted, so you limit who can relay.
rubricPoints: States that CUPS queues print jobs in a spool and feeds them to the printer, using IPP on port 631.
Names at least one CUPS command such as lp, lpstat or cancel and what it does.
Defines the MTA as the server that relays mail over SMTP on port 25, distinct from the MUA and MDA.
Explains that undeliverable mail waits in a queue and is retried, viewable with mailq.
Names a risk such as an open relay or an exposed listening port, and how to limit it.

suggested.rationale: This objective is conceptual knowledge of service roles, ports and commands, and no current mission or planned engine exercises printing or mail.

lessons.plain: Systematic troubleshooting is a fixed, repeatable order of steps for fixing a broken system, so that you follow evidence instead of guessing. You first pin down exactly what is wrong. Then you form a likely explanation, test it, plan a fix, apply it, check that everything truly works, and write down what happened. Think of a doctor: they ask about symptoms, form a likely diagnosis, run a test to confirm it, then treat, then check you recovered. They do not hand out random pills hoping one works. The same discipline keeps a Linux server from getting worse while you fix it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server stopped answering this morning. Before you change anything at all, what two or three questions would you want answered first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A troubleshooting methodology is an ordered set of steps that turns a vague complaint into a confirmed root cause. The root cause is the underlying reason for the failure. A symptom is only the visible effect. A common version of the steps is: identify the problem, form a theory of probable cause, test the theory, plan the fix, implement it, verify full functionality, and document what you found.

This works because each step narrows the search. Identifying the problem means gathering facts. What exactly fails? Since when? What changed recently? Who is affected? A theory is a guess you can test against evidence. Testing it with read-only commands tells you whether you are right before you touch anything. If the theory is wrong, you form a new one and test again.

Worked example: users report the website is down. Identify: you run systemctl status nginx. systemctl is the tool that controls services, and nginx is the web server. It shows the service as failed, and you learn a package update ran last night. Theory: something now blocks nginx from starting. Test: journalctl -u nginx, which shows that one service's log messages, reports that the address is already in use. Then ss -tlnp, which lists listening network ports and the programs that own them, shows another web server holding port 80. The theory is confirmed. Plan: disable the stray service, and note that this briefly affects nothing else. Implement: stop and disable it, then start nginx. Verify: request the page locally and confirm users can load it. Document: record that the update installed a second web server that took the port.

A common mistake is jumping straight to a fix, such as rebooting or changing several settings at once. A reboot can wipe the evidence and hide the cause. Changing many things at once means you never learn which change mattered. On a running system, the outage then returns, often at a worse time.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic's appointment app stopped saving bookings this morning. Identify: staff at all three front desks are affected, it started at 8:00, and a colleague edited the app's database connection setting yesterday evening. Theory: the edited setting now points the app at the wrong database port. Test: ??? Plan: put back the previous port value during the lunch break, when no bookings are made. Implement: restore the value and restart the app's service. Verify: book a test appointment at each desk and confirm it saves. Document: record that yesterday's edit changed the port. Which action belongs in the missing Test step?
choices: Read the app service's log messages with journalctl -u, without changing anything, to check which port it is failing to reach
Change the port, the database password and the timeout together so every likely cause is covered at once
Reboot the server first so the app starts from a clean state before you look any further
Restore the old port value right away and restart the service to see if bookings start saving again
questions.why: Testing means checking the theory against evidence with read-only commands before touching anything, and the service's log can confirm or rule out the wrong-port theory.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company's nightly backup job fails with the message "no space left on device." Investigation shows the disk filled up because a log file grew huge after someone left a verbose debug setting switched on last week. Which of these is the root cause?
choices: The "no space left on device" message
The nightly backup job failing to finish
The debug setting that was left switched on
The disk being completely full
questions.why: The root cause is the underlying reason for the failure; the error message, the failed job and the full disk are all visible effects, or symptoms, that follow from the debug setting being left on.

questions.prompt: At a law firm, the shared print service stops sending jobs to printers. Your theory is that the print service has crashed, but systemctl status shows it is active and running normally. Following a systematic methodology, what should you do next?
choices: Restart the print service anyway, since that usually fixes printing
Plan the fix for a crashed service as originally intended
Form a new theory of probable cause and test it against evidence
Document that the service was running and close the ticket
questions.why: When testing shows a theory is wrong, the methodology says to form a new theory and test it, rather than acting on a disproved guess or stopping early.

questions.prompt: A university lab server loses network access. In a hurry, a technician changes a firewall rule, a DNS (name lookup) setting and a network card setting all at once, and the server comes back online. What is the main problem with this approach?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because the server is now working and that was the goal
It breaks the network card setting, which can never be changed while the server runs
No one knows which change fixed it, so the cause is unknown and the outage may return
It skips the Identify step, which only matters for problems affecting many users
questions.why: Changing many things at once means you never learn which change mattered, so the real cause stays hidden and the failure can come back, often at a worse time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, the steps you follow when a Linux service breaks, and describe one limit or tradeoff of working this methodically during a live outage.
lessons.modelAnswer: I don't start by changing things. First I pin down the problem. What exactly fails, since when, who is affected, and what changed recently? Then I form a theory about the likely cause and test it with read-only commands. I check the service status and its logs, or I look at which program holds a port. If the evidence doesn't fit, I drop that theory and try another. Once it's confirmed, I plan the fix and think about its side effects. I change one thing at a time, then verify the whole service works for real users, not just that the process started. Finally I write down the cause and the fix. The tradeoff is time. During a big outage you may need a quick workaround first, like a restart or a rollback. That can destroy evidence, so I capture logs and status before I do it, then come back for the root cause.
rubricPoints: Names the ordered steps: identify, theorize, test, plan, implement, verify, document.
Distinguishes a symptom from the root cause.
Tests theories with evidence such as status output and logs before changing anything.
Changes one thing at a time and verifies full functionality afterward.
Names a tradeoff, such as speed versus preserving evidence during an outage.

suggested.rationale: This mission walks the learner through the full cycle: gather evidence on a failing service, confirm the cause, apply a fix, then restart and verify.

lessons.plain: Diagnosing a boot failure means working out which step of start-up broke when a Linux machine will not come up normally. Starting a computer is like a relay race. The firmware hands off to a boot loader, the boot loader hands off to the kernel, and the kernel hands off to the service manager. If you know which runner dropped the baton, you know where to look. Rescue mode, also called single-user mode, is a stripped-down start. It gives you one administrator shell with almost nothing else running, so you can repair the system from the inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server stops partway through start-up after someone edited the file that lists which disks to attach. It shows a message offering a maintenance shell. Before any teaching, guess why the system started that far but refused to finish.
lessons.teach:
Linux boots in stages. Firmware (BIOS or UEFI, the built-in chip software) finds a disk and runs the boot loader, usually GRUB2, a small program that loads the kernel. The kernel is the core of the operating system. It also loads the initramfs, a tiny temporary filesystem holding the drivers needed to reach the real root filesystem. The kernel then starts systemd, the service manager, which brings the system up to a target. A target is a named group of services, such as multi-user.target for a normal server.

The symptom tells you the stage. No GRUB menu points to firmware or boot-loader trouble. A "kernel panic" message, meaning the kernel hit a fatal error, or "unable to mount root" points to the kernel or initramfs. Stopping after the kernel loads points to systemd, services or mounts.

To get in, press e at the GRUB menu and add a parameter to the line that starts with linux. Adding systemd.unit=rescue.target starts a minimal system: local disks are mounted, but there is no network and no normal services. Adding systemd.unit=emergency.target is even smaller: you get a shell with root mounted read-only. Adding rd.break stops inside the initramfs, which is used for jobs such as resetting a lost root password.

Worked example: someone mistyped a disk UUID (the unique ID of a partition) in /etc/fstab, the file listing filesystems to mount at boot. Here is how you would trace it.

1. Boot halts and drops into emergency mode.
2. You log in as root.
3. You run journalctl -xb, which shows this boot's log, and see a mount timing out.
4. You run mount -o remount,rw / to make root writable.
5. You run blkid, which lists the real UUIDs, and you correct fstab. You can add the nofail option to mounts that are not essential.
6. You run mount -a to test the file, then reboot.

A common mistake is editing files while root is still read-only, or rebooting again and again hoping it clears. On a live server, a boot failure usually means SSH never starts. You will need console access to repair it.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic's records server stops partway through booting after a technician changes some service settings. Trace the diagnosis. Step 1: The GRUB menu (the boot loader's menu) appears normally, so the firmware found the disk and the boot loader ran. Step 2: Kernel messages scroll past with no kernel panic, then systemd (the service manager) begins starting services, and the boot halts there. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: To investigate with local disks mounted but no network or normal services, the technician presses e at the GRUB menu and adds systemd.unit=rescue.target to the line starting with linux. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Conclude that the fault lies after the kernel loads, in systemd, a service or a mount
Conclude that nothing can be diagnosed yet, so reboot a few more times to see if it clears
Conclude that the firmware cannot find the disk, so the problem sits before the boot loader runs
Conclude that the initramfs is missing a driver, so the kernel cannot reach the real root filesystem
questions.why: Because the boot loader ran and the kernel loaded without a panic before the halt, the failure belongs to the systemd, services and mounts stage.

questions.prompt: A warehouse's inventory server shows a "kernel panic" message during startup, which means the kernel hit a fatal error. Which boot stage should you investigate first?
choices: The kernel or the initramfs, the temporary filesystem holding root drivers
The firmware, because it failed to find a bootable disk
The network settings, because SSH could not be reached
The systemd targets, because a normal service failed to start
questions.why: A kernel panic or an "unable to mount root" message points to the kernel or initramfs stage, not to firmware or systemd.

questions.prompt: A bakery's order server boots into emergency mode. You log in as root and try to fix a line in a configuration file, but the save fails. What should you run before editing files?
choices: journalctl -xb, to make the log writable
mount -a, to mount every filesystem as writable
blkid, to unlock the root partition
mount -o remount,rw /, to make root writable
questions.why: Emergency mode mounts root read-only, so you must remount it read-write before any edit can be saved.

questions.prompt: A cloud-hosted web server for a travel agency was rebooted and now cannot be reached over SSH. The boot appears to be failing. What is the most sensible next move?
choices: Keep rebooting the server until the boot problem clears by itself
Reinstall SSH remotely, because the SSH package must be broken
Wait for the network to come back, since SSH failures are network faults
Use the provider's console access to watch the boot and repair it
questions.why: A boot failure usually means SSH never starts, so you need console access to see the failure and fix it, and repeated reboots will not help.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between rescue.target, emergency.target and rd.break when a server will not boot. Include one limit or tradeoff of these modes.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I read where the boot stops. If it reaches systemd but a service or mount fails, I use rescue.target. It mounts local filesystems and gives me a root shell, which is enough for most repairs. If even mounting fails, for example because of a bad fstab entry, I use emergency.target. It mounts only root, and read-only, so I remount it read-write before editing. If I cannot log in at all, such as with a lost root password, or the problem is before the real root is mounted, I use rd.break to stop inside the initramfs. The tradeoff is that these modes run almost nothing: no networking and no normal services. So I need console access, not SSH, and I cannot test the application properly until a normal boot. They also give a full root shell to anyone at the console, so physical and console access must be protected.
rubricPoints: Identifies the boot stage from the symptom: firmware, GRUB, kernel/initramfs or systemd.
Explains that kernel parameters are added by editing the GRUB entry.
Distinguishes rescue.target, emergency.target and rd.break by how much of the system they start.
Notes that root may be read-only and must be remounted read-write before editing.
Names a limit, such as no network or SSH, the need for console access, or the security exposure.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine simulates a broken boot, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios to pick the stage and the right mode adds the most.

lessons.plain: A Linux disk can stop accepting new files for three different reasons, and each needs a different fix. It can run out of space, meaning the bytes are used up. It can run out of inodes, the small index records Linux keeps for every file, even when plenty of space remains. Or the drive itself can be physically failing. Think of a library: the shelves can be full, the card catalogue can run out of cards while shelves sit half empty, or the building can be crumbling. Diagnosing storage means checking each possibility in turn instead of guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application reports 'No space left on device', yet a quick check shows the disk is only 40% full. What could possibly be running out besides raw space?
lessons.teach:
Storage diagnosis means working out whether a filesystem is short of space, short of inodes, or sitting on failing hardware. A filesystem is the structure that organises files on a disk partition. An inode is a fixed-size record holding one file's metadata, such as owner, permissions and where its data lives. Each filesystem gets a set number of inodes when it is created, so millions of tiny files can use them all up while disk space remains.

Start with df -h, which shows the space used on each mounted filesystem in human-readable units. Next run df -i, which shows inode use. Then narrow the cause. du -sh /var/* totals the space used under each directory, so you can find what is consuming it. For inode problems, count files per directory with a command like find /var -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f3 | sort | uniq -c. For hardware, run dmesg or journalctl -k to read kernel messages and look for I/O errors. Then run smartctl -a /dev/sda, which reads the drive's built-in self-monitoring health data, called SMART, including reallocated or pending sectors. A filesystem that suddenly becomes read-only is also a classic sign that the kernel detected errors and stopped writing to protect the data.

Worked example. Writes fail with 'No space left on device'. df -h shows / at 40% used. df -i shows / at 100% inode use. Counting files per directory points to /var. Drilling deeper finds about two million tiny session files in one cache folder. You delete the stale ones, df -i drops to 30%, and writes succeed again.

Common mistake: deleting a huge log file while a process still has it open. The name disappears, but the space is not freed until that process closes the file, so df still shows the disk as full. Run lsof +L1 to list deleted files that are still held open. Then restart or signal that process, or truncate the file instead of deleting it. On a running server, an untreated full disk crashes databases, stops logging and blocks logins.

questions.prompt:
A small accounting firm's file server stores shared documents on /data, which lives on the disk /dev/sdb. Staff can open files but every save fails. Here is the investigation so far, with one step missing.

Step 1: df -h shows /data at 62% used, so space is not the problem.
Step 2: df -i shows /data at 18% inode use, so inodes are not the problem either.
Step 3: The filesystem has suddenly switched to read-only, which suggests the kernel detected errors and stopped writing to protect the data.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: smartctl -a /dev/sdb reports 140 reallocated sectors and 12 pending sectors. The drive is failing, so you back up the data and replace the disk.

What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Count files per directory with find /data -xdev -type f to find where inodes are being used up
Run du -sh /data/* to total the space used under each directory and find what is consuming the disk
Run lsof +L1 to list deleted files that a process still holds open
Run dmesg or journalctl -k to read kernel messages and look for I/O errors on the disk
questions.why: With space and inodes both healthy and the filesystem gone read-only, the next step is to check the kernel messages for I/O errors, which points toward failing hardware before you confirm it with SMART data.

questions.prompt: A build server's /builds filesystem refuses new files with 'No space left on device', yet df -h shows it only 35% full. Which explanation fits these symptoms?
choices: The drive's SMART data must be reporting pending sectors, which always shows up as 'No space left on device'
The kernel has made the filesystem read-only, and that always produces a 35% reading in df -h
df -h rounds its numbers, so the real usage is close to 100% and the figure shown is misleading
The filesystem has run out of inodes, the fixed-size records each file needs, because their number was set when the filesystem was created
questions.why: Each file needs one inode, and a filesystem has a fixed number of them, so many small files can use up every inode while plenty of disk space remains.

questions.prompt: On a video hosting server, /home is at 98% used. An admin deletes a 30 GB export file that a running transcoding process was still writing to. Afterwards, df -h still shows /home at 98%. What is the best next step?
choices: Run df -i, because the space must now be held by inodes instead of data
Run lsof +L1 to find the deleted file still held open, then restart or signal the transcoding process so the space is freed
Run smartctl -a on the disk, because space that will not free up means the drive is failing
Delete more files, because df -h only updates after the disk drops below 95%
questions.why: A deleted file's space is not freed while a process keeps it open, and lsof +L1 lists those files so you can make the process close them.

questions.prompt: A payroll application's /srv filesystem is failing writes. df -h shows /srv at 99% used, and df -i shows only 20% inode use. Which command best narrows down what is using up the space?
choices: find /srv -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f3 | sort | uniq -c to count files per directory
smartctl -a /dev/sda to read the drive's health data
du -sh /srv/* to total the space used under each directory
df -i again to confirm whether inode use is rising
questions.why: The problem is space, not inodes, so du -sh totals the space under each directory and shows what is filling the filesystem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell a full disk, inode exhaustion and a failing drive apart, and name one trap where the obvious fix does not free space.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three can produce write failures, so I check each one in turn. First I run df -h. If a filesystem is near 100%, it is a space problem, and I use du -sh on directories to find what is consuming it. If df -h looks fine, I run df -i. Inodes are the per-file metadata records, and there is a fixed number of them, so millions of tiny files can exhaust them while space remains. In that case I count files per directory to find the culprit. If neither is full, or the filesystem has gone read-only, I suspect hardware. I check dmesg or journalctl -k for I/O errors and run smartctl to read the drive's SMART health data. The trap is deleting a big log that a process still holds open. The space stays used until that process closes the file, so I check lsof +L1 and restart the process or truncate the file instead.
rubricPoints: Uses df -h for space and df -i for inodes and explains the difference.
Defines an inode as per-file metadata with a fixed count per filesystem.
Uses du or file counting to locate what is consuming space or inodes.
Checks kernel logs and SMART data with smartctl for a failing drive, noting a read-only remount as a sign.
Names the deleted-but-open file trap and lsof +L1 or truncation as the fix.

suggested.rationale: The disk-full mission has the learner find what is consuming space and free it safely, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Diagnosing a network problem on Linux means finding which layer is broken instead of guessing. A connection depends on a chain: the network card is up and has an address, the system knows where to send traffic (a route), the far machine answers, the name you typed turns into an address (DNS, the internet's phone book), and a program is actually listening on the right port. Think of a letter that never arrived: was the envelope addressed, did the post office know the route, does the house exist, is anyone home? You check each link in order, and the first broken one is your culprit.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server can ping 8.8.8.8 successfully, but running a command against api.example.com fails with 'could not resolve host'. Which part of the chain do you suspect, and which parts can you probably rule out?
lessons.teach:
Network diagnosis means checking each layer of a connection in order, from the machine outward, until one check fails. It works because each layer depends on the one below, so the lowest failing layer is usually the root cause.

The tools: ip is the modern command for interfaces and routes. 'ip addr' shows each interface (network connection point) with its state and IP address, and 'ip route' shows the routing table, including the default gateway (the router that receives traffic for any network not otherwise listed). ping sends ICMP echo requests (small 'are you there' messages) and reports replies and round-trip time. traceroute lists every router (hop) between you and a destination, showing where packets stop. DNS resolution turns a hostname into an IP address; the system's DNS servers are listed in /etc/resolv.conf, and 'dig name' or 'getent hosts name' tests the lookup. ss shows sockets (open network endpoints); 'ss -tlnp' lists TCP ports that programs are listening on, with the owning process.

Worked example: users cannot reach a web app on this server. Step 1: 'ip addr' shows eth0 UP with 10.0.0.5, so the interface is fine. Step 2: 'ip route' shows a default via 10.0.0.1. Step 3: 'ping 10.0.0.1' replies, so the local network works. Step 4: 'dig app.example.com' returns the correct address, so DNS is fine. Step 5: 'ss -tlnp' shows nothing on port 443. The web service is not listening; the network was never the problem, and the fix is the service itself.

A common mistake is treating a failed ping as proof a host is down. Many firewalls block ICMP, so a host can ignore ping while serving traffic normally; confirm with ss on that host or a connection to the real port. Skipping layers wastes time in a running system: teams restart routers or edit firewalls while the actual fault, such as a wrong resolv.conf entry or a stopped service, keeps the outage going.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's point-of-sale terminal cannot reach its order server, orders.bakeryco.net. The technician checks each layer from the machine outward. Step 1: 'ip addr' shows ens3 UP with 172.16.8.40, so the interface is fine. Step 2: 'ip route' shows a default route via 172.16.8.1, so a gateway is configured. Step 3: 'ping 172.16.8.1' gets replies, so the local network works. Step 4: ??? Step 5: Looking in /etc/resolv.conf, the technician finds it lists 172.16.9.250, a DNS server that was shut down last month. Changing it to the current DNS server fixes the problem. Which Step 4 best fits this investigation?
choices: Run 'ss -tlnp' on the terminal and conclude the fault is there, because no web server is listening on the terminal itself
Restart the store's router, because the default gateway is the most likely cause whenever a server cannot be reached
Run 'dig orders.bakeryco.net' and see that the lookup gets no answer, which points to name resolution as the failing layer
Run 'ping orders.bakeryco.net', see it fail, and declare the order server down because it did not answer the ping
questions.why: The layers below DNS have already passed, so the next check is the hostname lookup, and a failed dig is what leads the technician to /etc/resolv.conf.

questions.prompt: On a file server, 'ip route' shows the line 'default via 192.168.50.254'. What does 192.168.50.254 represent?
choices: The file server's own IP address on its main interface
The address of the last hop that traceroute will show before any destination
The DNS server the system uses to turn hostnames into IP addresses
The default gateway: the router that receives traffic for any network not otherwise listed in the routing table
questions.why: In 'ip route' output, the default route names the gateway, which is the router that handles traffic for any network that has no more specific route.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, 'ping 10.20.30.7' to the database server gets no replies at all. But the reporting app on another machine is still reading from that database normally. What is the best next step?
choices: Declare the database server down and start a failover, because a failed ping proves the host is unreachable
Restart the network router between the two machines, because ping traffic must be getting lost there
Check 'ss -tlnp' on the database server, or test a connection to the database's real port, because a firewall may simply be blocking ICMP
Edit /etc/resolv.conf on the database server, because a failed ping always means DNS is broken
questions.why: Many firewalls block ICMP echo requests, so a host can ignore ping while serving traffic normally; checking the listening port or connecting to it confirms whether the service is really up.

questions.prompt: From a warehouse server, 'traceroute supplier-portal.example.org' shows replies from hops 1 through 4. From hop 5 onward it shows only asterisks, meaning there were no replies. Local checks with 'ip addr', 'ip route' and a ping to the gateway all succeeded. What does this result suggest?
choices: Packets are stopping after hop 4, so the problem lies at or beyond that point in the path, not on the local machine
The supplier portal's web service is not listening on its port
The warehouse server's own network interface is down
DNS resolution failed, because traceroute only shows asterisks when a hostname cannot be looked up
questions.why: traceroute lists each router between you and the destination, so the place where replies stop shows roughly where packets are failing, and the local checks have already passed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out why a Linux server cannot reach a remote service, naming the order of checks and one limit of a tool you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I work from the machine outward so the first failing check points at the root cause. First 'ip addr' to confirm the interface is up with an address, then 'ip route' to confirm there is a default gateway. Next I ping the gateway and then the remote IP to test reachability, and if that fails I run traceroute to see which hop the packets stop at. Separately I test DNS with dig or getent and check /etc/resolv.conf, because pinging by IP can succeed while name lookups fail. Finally, on the server side, 'ss -tlnp' tells me whether anything is listening on the expected port. The limit: ping and traceroute rely on ICMP, which firewalls often block, so silence does not prove the host is down; I confirm by testing the real service port.
rubricPoints: Checks layers in order: interface and address, route, reachability, DNS, listening port.
Uses ip addr and ip route for local configuration and the default gateway.
Uses ping for reachability and traceroute to locate where packets stop.
Tests DNS separately, distinguishing name failures from connectivity failures.
Uses ss to confirm a service is actually listening on the expected port.
Notes that blocked ICMP means a failed ping does not prove a host is down.

suggested.rationale: No current mission covers network faults, and a path tracer would let the learner check interfaces, routes, hops and listeners layer by layer to find the broken link.

lessons.plain: When a Linux server feels slow, you need to know what it is short of. Usually that is processor time or memory. Tools like top and htop show a live view of which programs are busy and how stretched the machine is. Think of a coffee shop. The baristas are the processor cores. The queue at the counter is the load. The counter space is memory. When the counter is full, staff start stacking cups in the back room. That back room is swap: it works, but every trip there is slow. Your job is to read these signs and name the real bottleneck.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server has 4 processor cores and reports a load average of 8. Without any teaching, what do you think that number says about how busy the machine is?
lessons.teach:
top is a command that shows a live, refreshing table of running processes plus a summary header. htop is a friendlier version with colour, scrolling and a bar for each core. Both expose three key signals.

Load average is the average number of processes running on a CPU, waiting for one, or stuck waiting on disk. It is shown over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it to the number of CPU cores (independent processors, reported by nproc). Load equal to the core count means the CPUs are fully busy. Load above it means work is queuing.

RAM is the fast working memory programs use. Swap is disk space the kernel borrows as overflow when RAM runs short. Disk is far slower than RAM, so heavy swapping makes everything crawl. The free -h command shows memory totals. Its 'available' column estimates how much RAM programs can still get. That figure includes page cache, which is idle RAM Linux uses to hold recently read files and hands back on demand.

Worked example: users report a slow server.
1. nproc says 4.
2. top shows load average 7.90, 6.10, 2.30. The 1-minute figure is about double the cores, so work is queuing.
3. The values fall from left to right, so load rose recently.
4. In the header, %wa (I/O wait, time CPUs sit idle waiting on disk) is low and us (user CPU time) is high. That means CPU pressure, not disk.
5. The top process shows 380% CPU, nearly all four cores. That is the suspect.
6. free -h shows plenty available and little swap used, which rules out memory.

If load were high but CPU mostly idle with high %wa, the bottleneck would be disk instead.

Common mistake: panicking because the 'free' column is small. A small 'free' with a large 'available' is healthy caching. The real warning signs are low available memory, growing swap use, and nonzero si/so columns in vmstat (a command that reports pages swapped in and out per second). If real exhaustion is ignored, the kernel's OOM (out-of-memory) killer terminates a process, often your main service.

questions.prompt:
A small accounting firm's file server feels sluggish. Most of the diagnosis is done; one step is missing.
Step 1: nproc reports 8 cores.
Step 2: top shows load average 12.40, 12.10, 11.90. The 1-minute figure is about 1.5 times the core count, so work is queuing.
Step 3: The three values are nearly equal, so the high load has lasted at least 15 minutes rather than just starting.
Step 4: The top header shows %wa (I/O wait) at 65 and us (user CPU time) at 5. [MISSING: what does this mean?]
Step 5: free -h shows 9 GB available out of 16 GB and almost no swap used, which rules out memory.
Which conclusion belongs in Step 4?
choices: Memory is exhausted and the server is swapping heavily, so add RAM.
The CPUs are mostly sitting idle while waiting on disk, so the bottleneck is disk I/O.
The server is healthy, because the CPUs are mostly idle and a load of 12 is normal.
The CPUs are overloaded by a busy program, so look for the process using the most CPU.
questions.why: High %wa with low user time means the CPUs are waiting on disk rather than computing, so the high load points to a disk bottleneck.

questions.prompt: On a 16-core analytics server, nproc reports 16 and top shows load average 4.10, 4.00, 3.95. What does this tell you about CPU capacity?
choices: Work is queuing, because any load above 1.0 means the CPUs are overloaded.
Load has been rising sharply over the last few minutes.
The CPUs have plenty of spare capacity, because the load is well below the 16-core count.
The CPUs are exactly fully busy, with no spare capacity.
questions.why: Load is only a problem compared with the core count, and a load of about 4 on 16 cores means the CPUs are far from fully busy.

questions.prompt: A junior admin on a web host runs free -h and sees: total 32G, free 400M, available 22G, swap used 0B. They want to restart services to free up memory. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Memory is healthy. Most of the RAM is page cache that Linux hands back on demand, and 22 GB is still available.
Memory is nearly exhausted, because only 400 MB is free.
The server is swapping heavily, because free memory is so low.
The OOM killer is about to terminate a process, so restart services now.
questions.why: A small 'free' figure alongside a large 'available' figure is normal file caching, and with no swap in use there is no memory pressure.

questions.prompt: On a ticketing server, free -h shows the 'available' figure shrinking hour by hour, swap use keeps growing, and vmstat shows nonzero si and so values. If nobody acts, what is the most likely outcome?
choices: The kernel's OOM (out-of-memory) killer will terminate a process, often the main service.
Nothing serious will happen, because swap is a full replacement for RAM.
Load average will fall, because swapping moves work off the CPUs.
Linux will empty the page cache, and that will permanently fix the shortage.
questions.why: Shrinking available memory, growing swap use and nonzero si/so are the real signs of memory exhaustion, and if it continues the OOM killer ends a process to recover memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use top or htop, load average and free to decide whether a slow server is short of CPU, memory or disk. Include one limit of load average as a signal.
lessons.modelAnswer:
First I check how many cores the box has with nproc. Then I read the load average in top or htop. If the 1-minute figure is well above the core count, work is queuing. If the 1-minute figure is higher than the 15-minute one, the problem is recent.

Next I look at the CPU line. High user time means real CPU pressure, and the process list sorted by CPU shows the culprit. Low CPU use with high %wa means processes are waiting on disk.

For memory I use free -h and trust 'available', not 'free'. Linux fills spare RAM with cache on purpose. Growing swap use and nonzero si/so in vmstat show genuine memory pressure.

The limit: load average counts processes waiting on disk too. So high load alone does not prove a CPU shortage, and it means nothing until you compare it to the core count.
rubricPoints: Compares load average to the number of CPU cores rather than reading it in isolation.
Uses the 1-, 5- and 15-minute values to tell whether load is rising or falling.
Distinguishes CPU pressure from I/O wait using the CPU breakdown.
Trusts 'available' memory over 'free' because Linux uses idle RAM as cache.
Treats growing swap use and active swapping as the real memory warning sign.
Names a limit, such as load including disk-waiting processes.

suggested.rationale: In this mission the learner uses top-style tools and load readings to find what is burning the CPU, which is exactly this skill.

lessons.plain: A system log is a running diary that a Linux machine and its programs write as they work: what started, what stopped, what went wrong, and when. When something breaks, the log usually already contains the clue, but buried among thousands of ordinary lines. Reading logs for root cause means narrowing that diary to the right time and the right program, then finding the first real error rather than the noisy errors that follow it. Think of a flight recorder: after a crash, investigators do not read every second of the flight, they jump to the moments just before things went wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service failed at 14:02 and the log shows fifty error lines between 14:02 and 14:05. Which line do you think is most likely to point to the actual cause, and why?
lessons.teach:
System logs are timestamped records of events written by the kernel, services and applications. On most modern Linux systems, systemd-journald (the logging service that comes with systemd, the program that starts and manages services) collects these messages into the journal, a structured binary log. You read the journal with journalctl. Many programs also write plain-text files under /var/log, such as /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages for general events, /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure for logins, and application-specific files.

The skill is filtering. Useful journalctl options: -u name.service shows one unit (a service systemd manages); --since and --until limit the time window; -p err shows only priority error and worse (priority is the severity level, from emerg down to debug); -b shows the current boot and -b -1 the previous boot; -f follows new lines live; -k shows kernel messages, which you can also read with dmesg. For text files, grep searches for a word, tail -n 50 shows the last lines and tail -f follows them.

Why this works: failures cascade. One root problem triggers many downstream errors, so the earliest relevant error in the right window is usually closest to the cause.

Worked example: nginx is down. Step 1, systemctl status nginx shows it failed at 09:14. Step 2, journalctl -u nginx --since 09:10 shows repeated 'restart' messages, then 'bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (Address already in use)'. Step 3, that earliest error names the cause: another process holds port 80. Later lines like 'start request repeated too quickly' are symptoms of the repeated restart attempts, not the cause.

Common mistake: grabbing the last or loudest error and fixing that. You end up treating a symptom, and the service fails again. Another trap is reading the wrong boot; after a crash and reboot, the evidence is in the previous boot, so use -b -1. In a running system, misreading logs means repeated outages and changes that hide the real fault.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic runs its booking system as a service called bookingd.service on one Linux server. Nobody has rebooted the server today. Staff report bookings stopped working around 14:30.

Step 1: systemctl status bookingd shows the service entered the failed state at 14:32.
Step 2: ________
Step 3: The output shows, in order: at 14:27 'could not connect to database at 10.0.4.9:5432 (connection refused)', then several restart messages, then at 14:32 'start request repeated too quickly'.
Step 4: The earliest relevant error points at the cause. The booking service cannot reach its database, so the database server is where to look next. The 14:32 line is only a symptom of the repeated restarts.

Which command belongs in step 2?
choices: journalctl -b -1 -u bookingd
journalctl -f -k
journalctl -u bookingd --since 14:20
tail -n 50 /var/log/auth.log
questions.why: Filtering to the one unit and to a window that starts shortly before the 14:32 failure reveals the earlier 14:27 error that names the cause, whereas the previous boot, the login log, or live kernel messages would not show this service's history from today.

questions.prompt: An engineer runs journalctl -p err on a file server. Which messages will the output include?
choices: Only messages written by the kernel at error priority
Only messages at exactly the error priority, nothing more or less severe
Messages at error priority and every more severe level, up to emerg
Messages at error priority and every less severe level, down to debug
questions.why: The -p err option shows priority error and worse, meaning error plus the more severe levels above it toward emerg.

questions.prompt: A warehouse's inventory server crashed at about 03:00 and came back up on its own after a reboot. At 08:00 you want to find out what went wrong before the crash. Which command is the best starting point?
choices: journalctl -b
journalctl -f
dmesg
journalctl -b -1
questions.why: Evidence from before a crash and reboot lives in the previous boot, which -b -1 shows, while -b, dmesg and -f show only the current boot or new lines.

questions.prompt:
A print-management service called printq.service on a school's server keeps failing. Its journal for the last 15 minutes shows these lines in order:

11:02 'write to /var/spool/printq/job4471 failed: No space left on device'
11:02 'job queue corrupted, aborting'
11:03 'printq.service: Main process exited, status=1/FAILURE'
11:05 'printq.service: start request repeated too quickly'

What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The job queue file is corrupted and needs rebuilding
The service is set to restart too quickly
The main process has a bug that makes it exit with status 1
The disk holding the print spool is full
questions.why: Failures cascade, so the earliest relevant error, running out of disk space, is closest to the cause, and the queue corruption, exit and restart messages are downstream symptoms of it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use the system logs to find why a service stopped, and name one limit of logs or one way they can mislead you.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I confirm when the service failed, using systemctl status. Then I narrow the logs to that service and a short window around the failure, for example journalctl -u myapp --since a few minutes before, and add -p err if it is noisy. If the machine rebooted, I check the previous boot with -b -1, and I look at kernel messages with journalctl -k or dmesg if the problem might be hardware or memory. I read forward in time and look for the first real error, because one fault causes a cascade, and the later messages are usually symptoms. The limit is that logs only show what something chose to record: if logging was off, the disk was full, or the journal is not persistent across reboots, the evidence may be missing. A quiet log does not prove nothing went wrong.
rubricPoints: Narrows logs by service or unit and by a time window around the failure.
Names the right tools: journalctl with filters, and /var/log text files with grep or tail.
Looks for the earliest relevant error, treating later errors as cascading symptoms.
Checks the previous boot or kernel messages when a crash or reboot is involved.
States a limit, such as missing, non-persistent or noisy logs that can mislead.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner dig through real logs to find why an API is failing, which is exactly this skill.

lessons.plain: User authentication hardening means making it hard for someone to log in as a person they are not, and limiting what a real user can do once logged in. Password policies set the rules: how long and varied a password must be, how often it must change, and how many wrong guesses lock the account. Sudo is a tool that lets an approved person run specific admin commands with elevated power, using their own password, while keeping a record of who did what. Think of an office building. The badge rules stop strangers getting in. The key cabinet hands out only the keys a job needs, and it logs every key taken.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a whole team shares one root password, and something on the server gets deleted by accident, how would you find out who did it? What would you change so that next time you could tell?
lessons.teach:
Authentication hardening has two halves. The first makes logins hard to fake. The second limits what a legitimate user can do once inside.

A password policy is the set of rules a password must meet and how long it stays valid. Quality rules are usually enforced by PAM, the Pluggable Authentication Modules framework that login programs consult to decide whether a user may get in. Quality rules include a minimum length, a mix of character types, and no reuse of recent passwords. The pam_pwquality module checks new passwords against these rules. The pam_faillock module locks an account after a set number of failed attempts, which slows down guessing. Aging rules cover the maximum days before a forced change and the warning days before it. Defaults for new accounts live in /etc/login.defs, and the chage command sets them per user.

sudo lets an approved user run a command as another user, usually root, the all-powerful admin account, after typing their own password. Every use is logged, so actions trace back to a person rather than to a shared root password. Rules live in /etc/sudoers and in drop-in files under /etc/sudoers.d. Each rule says who, on which host, as which user, and which commands.

Worked example: operator dana must only restart the web server.
Step 1: run visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/dana. This opens a safe editor that checks syntax before saving.
Step 2: add the rule dana ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx.
Step 3: dana runs sudo systemctl restart nginx and types her own password. The command runs, and the log records it.
Step 4: dana tries sudo cat /etc/shadow, the file holding password hashes. sudo refuses and logs the attempt.

A common mistake is editing /etc/sudoers in a plain editor. One typo makes the file unreadable, and sudo stops working for everyone. If direct root login is also disabled, fixing it can require console recovery. Granting ALL or NOPASSWD for convenience is also risky: one stolen account then becomes full root control.

Together, these controls defend against guessed or reused passwords and shrink the damage a compromised account can do.

questions.prompt:
At a small public library, technician Omar must be allowed to restart the database service and nothing else. sudo is the tool that lets an approved user run a command as another user, usually root (the all-powerful admin account), after typing their own password. Here is the hardening pass, with one step missing.
Step 1: The admin runs visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/omar. visudo is a safe editor that checks syntax before saving. Files under /etc/sudoers.d are drop-in rule files that sudo reads alongside /etc/sudoers.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Omar runs sudo systemctl restart postgresql and types his own password. The restart runs and is logged.
Step 4: Omar tries sudo systemctl stop firewalld. sudo refuses and logs the attempt.
Which line belongs in Step 2?
choices: omar ALL=(ALL) ALL
omar ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl
omar ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart postgresql
root ALL=(omar) /usr/bin/systemctl restart postgresql
questions.why: This rule names who (omar), the host (ALL), the target user (root) and exactly one command, so the restart works and every other command is refused, as Step 4 shows.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm notices bots trying thousands of passwords against staff accounts. It wants each account locked after 5 failed login attempts to slow the guessing down. Which piece of the system does this job? (PAM, the Pluggable Authentication Modules framework, is what login programs consult to decide whether a user may get in.)
choices: The chage command
The pam_pwquality module
The pam_faillock module
The /etc/login.defs file
questions.why: pam_faillock is the PAM module that locks an account after a set number of failed attempts. pam_pwquality checks the quality of new passwords, while chage and /etc/login.defs deal with password aging.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, only the account for receptionist Lee must be forced to change its password every 60 days, with a warning 10 days before the deadline. Other accounts keep their current settings. Password aging means the rules for how long a password stays valid. What is the right tool for this?
choices: The chage command, which sets aging rules for one user
visudo, which safely edits sudo rules
The pam_pwquality module, which checks password strength
A new rule file under /etc/sudoers.d
questions.why: chage sets aging values, such as maximum days and warning days, for an individual user. /etc/login.defs holds defaults for new accounts, and the sudo tools control command privileges, not passwords.

questions.prompt: On a print-shop server, direct root login is disabled. An admin opens /etc/sudoers in a plain text editor instead of visudo, makes a typo and saves the file. What is the most likely result?
choices: sudo stops working for everyone, and fixing it may require console recovery
Only the admin who made the typo loses sudo access
The plain editor warns about the syntax error and refuses to save
sudo skips the broken line and keeps applying the other rules
questions.why: A single typo can make the sudoers file unreadable, which breaks sudo for all users. With direct root login also disabled, there may be no normal way back in, so console recovery can be needed. visudo prevents this by checking syntax before saving.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we bother with password rules, account lockout and per-command sudo rules when we could just give admins the root password. Explain in your own words what each control defends against, and name one tradeoff or limit.
lessons.modelAnswer: Password quality rules, enforced through PAM with pam_pwquality, make passwords long and varied, so they are hard to guess or crack. Lockout with pam_faillock stops an attacker from trying thousands of guesses. Aging, set in login.defs or with chage, limits how long a leaked password stays useful. Sudo replaces a shared root password. Each admin uses their own password, and every elevated command is logged, so we know who did what. Rules in sudoers.d can limit a person to just the commands their job needs, so a stolen account cannot take over the whole server. We edit those rules with visudo, because a syntax error could break sudo for everyone. These controls have limits and costs. Strict rules and frequent forced changes push people to write passwords down. Lockout can be abused to lock real users out on purpose. Very narrow sudo rules mean more requests and more upkeep.
rubricPoints: Password quality and lockout rules defend against guessing and weak or reused passwords.
PAM modules enforce quality and lockout rules, while login.defs and chage handle password aging.
Sudo ties elevated actions to individual users and logs them, replacing a shared root password.
Least-privilege sudo rules limit the damage if one account is compromised.
Sudoers should be edited with visudo so a syntax error cannot break sudo.
The answer names a real tradeoff, such as user friction, lockout abuse or admin overhead.

suggested.rationale: No current mission has the learner configure PAM or sudoers, and reasoning through scenario-style cases best builds this skill, such as reading a sudoers line or picking the right lockout or aging control.

lessons.plain: A firewall is a gatekeeper that looks at every piece of network traffic arriving at or leaving a server and decides, using a list of rules, whether to let it through or block it. Think of a security desk in an office lobby. The guard checks each visitor against a guest list: expected visitors go in, and everyone else is turned away. On Linux, the kernel itself does the checking. Tools named iptables, nftables and firewalld are simply different ways for an administrator to write and manage that guest list.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server runs a website and you log in to it remotely over SSH. If you set the firewall to block everything that is not on an allow list, which kinds of incoming traffic would you put on that list, and what might happen if you forgot one?
lessons.teach:
A firewall filters network traffic by matching it against rules. Traffic travels in packets, which are small chunks of data. Each packet carries a destination port, a number that identifies which service it is meant for. SSH remote login normally uses port 22, and HTTPS websites use port 443. A rule says "if a packet matches these conditions, take this action," where the action is usually accept or drop.

Inside the Linux kernel, a filtering framework called netfilter applies the rules. Rules are grouped into chains, which are ordered lists checked at a particular point. INPUT covers traffic arriving for this machine, OUTPUT covers traffic it sends, and FORWARD covers traffic passing through it. Rules in a chain are checked from top to bottom, and the first rule that matches decides the outcome. If no rule matches, the chain's default policy applies. A safe baseline uses a default policy of drop on INPUT. The firewall is also stateful, which means connection tracking remembers conversations already in progress, so a rule can accept packets that belong to an established connection.

Three tools manage these rules. iptables is the older tool. nftables is its newer replacement, with one syntax that covers both IPv4 and IPv6. firewalld is a management service that sits on top of nftables. It groups rules into zones, which are named trust levels such as public. It also keeps two copies of its settings: runtime, which is active now, and permanent, which survives a reboot.

Worked example. INPUT has a default policy of drop, then rule 1 accepts established connections, rule 2 accepts TCP port 22, and rule 3 accepts TCP port 443. A new packet arrives for port 3306, which is a database port. It does not match rule 1, 2 or 3, so the default policy drops it. A reply from an update server that this machine contacted matches rule 1, so it is accepted.

Common mistake: switching INPUT to drop over a remote session before allowing port 22. Your own SSH connection is cut and you are locked out. A related mistake in firewalld is changing only the runtime settings, so the rules silently disappear at the next reboot.

questions.prompt:
A small print shop's file server has an INPUT chain with a default policy of accept. Rule 1 accepts packets that belong to established connections. Rule 2 drops TCP port 8080. Rule 3 accepts TCP port 8080. A brand-new connection attempt arrives for TCP port 8080.

Step 1: The packet starts a new conversation, so it does not belong to an established connection. Rule 1 does not match.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The packet is dropped, and rule 3 is never consulted.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Rule 2 is skipped because rule 3 accepts the same port, and an accept always outranks a drop.
No rule decides on its own, so the chain's default policy of accept settles the outcome.
Rule 2 matches the packet, so its drop action decides the outcome and checking stops there.
Rule 2 matches, but checking continues down the chain, and the last matching rule decides the outcome.
questions.why: Rules in a chain are checked from top to bottom and the first one that matches decides, so rule 2's drop ends the check before rule 3 is reached.

questions.prompt: A clinic's web server sends a request out to a time server. Its INPUT chain drops all new incoming traffic by default, yet the time server's reply still gets through because of a rule that accepts established connections. What firewall property makes this possible?
choices: The default policy of drop only applies to IPv6 traffic, so ordinary IPv4 replies pass through untouched.
The OUTPUT chain automatically copies its accept rules into INPUT for any address the machine has contacted.
The firewall is stateful: connection tracking remembers conversations already in progress, so replies to them can be accepted.
Replies are carried in zones rather than packets, so the INPUT chain does not inspect them at all.
questions.why: Connection tracking lets the firewall recognise packets that belong to an established conversation, so a single rule can accept those replies while new unsolicited traffic is still dropped.

questions.prompt: A logistics company sets up a Linux machine as a gateway. Traffic from office laptops passes through it on its way to the internet, and the machine itself is neither the sender nor the final destination. Which netfilter chain checks this pass-through traffic?
choices: FORWARD, because it covers traffic passing through the machine.
INPUT, because the traffic enters one of the gateway's network ports.
OUTPUT, because the traffic leaves the gateway toward the internet.
public, because that is the zone for untrusted internet traffic.
questions.why: FORWARD is the chain for traffic passing through a machine, while INPUT is for traffic meant for the machine itself and OUTPUT is for traffic it sends.

questions.prompt: An admin at a museum opens TCP port 8443 using firewalld and confirms visitors can reach the booking site. After a scheduled reboot that night, the site is unreachable and the port is closed again. What is the most likely cause?
choices: firewalld only accepts rules for ports 22 and 443, so port 8443 was rejected when the service restarted.
Connection tracking forgot the visitors' sessions at reboot, which deletes any rule that allowed them in.
The rule was added to the permanent settings, which wait until the next reboot before they apply.
The rule was added only to the runtime settings, which are active now but do not survive a reboot.
questions.why: firewalld keeps runtime settings that are active now and permanent settings that survive a reboot, so a change made only at runtime silently disappears at the next restart.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Linux host firewall decides whether to accept a packet, and why a default-drop policy is a good baseline. Name one limit or risk of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The kernel's netfilter framework checks each packet against chains of rules. INPUT is the chain for traffic coming into the box. Rules are read from top to bottom, and the first match wins. If nothing matches, the chain's default policy decides what happens. I set INPUT to drop by default and then explicitly allow only what the server needs, such as established connections, SSH on 22 and HTTPS on 443. That way any service someone starts by accident, like a database listening on 3306, cannot be reached from the network. iptables, nftables and firewalld are just different front ends to the same idea; firewalld adds zones and keeps separate runtime and permanent settings. The risk is that rule order and policy changes can lock you out if you drop traffic before allowing SSH. There is also a limit: a host firewall only controls which ports can be reached. It does not fix a vulnerable service you have deliberately exposed.
rubricPoints: Rules are checked in order and the first match decides.
The default policy applies when no rule matches, and drop on INPUT is the safe baseline.
Allow only the needed ports, such as 22 and 443, plus established connections through stateful tracking.
iptables, nftables and firewalld are tools over the same kernel filtering, and firewalld uses zones and separates runtime from permanent settings.
Names a risk or limit, such as SSH lockout, rules lost on reboot, or no protection for a service that is exposed on purpose.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet through ordered rules and a default policy, and spotting lockout or rules lost on reboot, is best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, since no current mission or planned engine has the learner edit a host firewall.

lessons.plain: Mandatory access control (MAC) is a second security gate built into the Linux kernel. Normal file permissions let the owner of a file decide who may use it. MAC adds a central rulebook, written by the administrator, that every program must also obey, even programs running as root. Think of an office building. Your door key (normal permissions) opens your office. Security staff still have a list saying the cafeteria cook may enter the kitchen and nowhere else. If someone steals the cook's key, the list still stops them. SELinux and AppArmor are the two common Linux tools that enforce such a rulebook.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server process is hijacked by an attacker, and the files it tries to read are world-readable. What kind of extra rule could still stop it from reading a password file it never needs?
lessons.teach:
Discretionary access control (DAC) is the classic Linux model: owner, group and other permission bits, set at the discretion of the file's owner. Root bypasses DAC entirely. Mandatory access control (MAC) is an extra layer where a system-wide policy, a set of rules loaded into the kernel, decides what each program may touch. A request must pass DAC and MAC; either one can deny it.

SELinux, common on Red Hat family systems, works with labels. A label, also called a security context, is a tag on every file and process. Its most important part is the type, for example httpd_t for the web server process and httpd_sys_content_t for web content. Type enforcement rules say which process types may do what to which file types. AppArmor, common on Ubuntu and SUSE, instead uses profiles: per-program rule files listing the paths that program may read, write or execute.

Both have modes. SELinux enforcing blocks and logs violations; permissive only logs; disabled turns it off. AppArmor has enforce and complain (log only). Denials are recorded in the audit log, usually /var/log/audit/audit.log for SELinux.

Worked example: you move the website to /srv/site and set permissions to 755. Pages return 403. Step one, permissions are fine, so suspect MAC. Step two, ls -Z shows the files carry the type var_t, not httpd_sys_content_t. Step three, the audit log shows an httpd_t denial for var_t. Step four, register the correct label for that path with semanage fcontext and apply it with restorecon. The site works, and the web server still cannot read anything outside its allowed types.

The common mistake is fixing such errors by switching to permissive or disabling SELinux. The site works, but you have removed the containment. On a running server, MAC means a compromised service is boxed into the files and actions its policy allows, which limits the damage of a break-in.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a label-printing service on Ubuntu with AppArmor in enforce mode. AppArmor confines each program with a profile, which is a per-program rule file listing the paths that program may read, write or execute.
