An admin moves the service's output folder to /data/labels and gives the service's user full write permission on it. The service now fails to save files.

Step 1: The ordinary owner/group/other permissions (discretionary access control) are correct, so suspect mandatory access control (MAC), the system-wide policy layer.
Step 2: The log shows an AppArmor denial for this program writing to /data/labels.
Step 3: The program's profile only allows writes to its old folder, /var/lib/labels.
Step 4: ???
Result: Labels save again, and the service still cannot write anywhere its profile does not allow.

Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Switch the program's profile to complain mode so the write is logged instead of blocked
Add a rule allowing writes to /data/labels to the program's profile and reload it
Run the label service as root so it can bypass the access checks
Set the permissions on /data/labels to 777 so every user can write there
questions.why: Allowing the new path in the profile fixes the denial while keeping the program confined to only the paths it is meant to use.

questions.prompt: On a Red Hat family server running SELinux, what does a type such as httpd_sys_content_t represent?
choices: The owner, group and other permission bits that the file's owner sets
The mode SELinux is running in, such as enforcing or permissive
The path of the per-program rule file that lists what a program may touch
The part of a file's or process's security label that type enforcement rules use to decide access
questions.why: In SELinux every file and process carries a label (security context), and its type is the key part that type enforcement rules match against.

questions.prompt: At a university, a backup program runs as root on a server with SELinux in enforcing mode. It is refused access to a file even though root normally ignores permission bits. What best explains the refusal?
choices: The file's owner set its permission bits to deny root
The MAC policy denied it; root bypasses DAC but a request must also pass MAC
Root never has access to files it did not create
SELinux in enforcing mode only logs violations, so something else blocked it
questions.why: Root skips discretionary checks, but mandatory access control is a separate layer, and either layer can deny a request.

questions.prompt: A hosting firm's mail service fails after a configuration change. To get it working fast, an admin sets SELinux to permissive and leaves it that way. What is the main consequence for the running server?
choices: The mail service is still blocked, because permissive mode denies everything
Denials stop being logged, so the audit log stays empty
Violations are only logged, so a compromised service is no longer boxed in by policy
All file permission bits are ignored until SELinux is set back to enforcing
questions.why: Permissive mode logs but does not block, so the containment that limits damage from a break-in is gone even though the service works.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a server needs SELinux or AppArmor when it already has file permissions, and name one tradeoff or limit of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: File permissions are discretionary: the owner sets them, and root ignores them. If an attacker takes over a service, they inherit whatever that service's user, or root, can reach. SELinux and AppArmor add mandatory access control, a kernel-enforced policy that confines each program to what it legitimately needs, whatever its user. SELinux does this with labels and type rules; AppArmor uses path-based profiles per program. So a hijacked web server can serve web content but cannot read shadow passwords or open odd network ports. The tradeoff is operational friction: moving files or changing a service's behaviour can trigger denials that look like permission bugs, and people are tempted to disable MAC. The right response is to read the audit log and fix labels or profiles, maybe testing in permissive or complain mode first. It also does not stop attacks within what the policy allows.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes DAC (owner-set permissions, bypassed by root) from MAC (central kernel-enforced policy).
States that MAC confines a compromised process, including root-run ones, limiting damage.
Describes SELinux as label/type based and AppArmor as path-based profiles.
Mentions modes such as enforcing/permissive or enforce/complain and the audit log for denials.
Names a tradeoff, such as unexpected denials or the temptation to disable it instead of relabeling.

suggested.rationale: No current mission exercises MAC, and the key exam skill is reasoning through a scenario where permissions look correct yet access is denied, then choosing to relabel rather than disable.

lessons.plain: File integrity and permission auditing means regularly checking two things on a server. First, have any important files changed when nobody meant to change them? Second, do any files give more people more access than they should? Think of a building manager who photographs every lock and every key on day one, then walks the halls each week comparing what they see to the photos. A lock that was swapped, or a master key left hanging by the front door, gets noticed. The auditing does not stop the break-in itself. It makes sure tampering and careless access do not stay hidden.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an attacker replaced the program /usr/bin/ls with a malicious copy that behaves normally. How could you discover the swap without trusting anything that ls itself shows you?
lessons.teach:
File integrity and permission auditing is the practice of checking whether files have changed unexpectedly and whether their permissions grant too much access.

Permissions first. Every file has an owner, a group, and "others", meaning everyone else. Each of these three can have read (worth 4), write (worth 2) and execute (worth 1). In octal notation, 640 means the owner can read and write, the group can read, and others get nothing. SUID (set-user-ID) is a special bit that makes a program run with its owner's privileges, so a SUID program owned by root runs as root. SGID does the same thing for the group. A world-writable file is one that others can write to. You hunt for risky files with find. The command find / -perm -4000 -type f lists SUID files, and find / -perm -0002 -type f lists world-writable files. Then you compare the results with what you expect to see.

Integrity second. A checksum, or hash, such as SHA-256 is a short fingerprint calculated from a file's contents. Changing even one byte changes the fingerprint. A file integrity monitoring tool such as AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) saves a baseline database of hashes, owners, permissions and timestamps. Later it rescans and reports any differences. Package managers can also check installed files against their original package: rpm -Va on Red Hat-family systems, and debsums on Debian-family systems.

Here is a worked example. Step 1: on a fresh server, run aide --init and move the new database into place. Step 2: a week later, run aide --check. Step 3: the report says the hash of /usr/bin/passwd changed, but no update was logged. Step 4: rpm -Vf /usr/bin/passwd also shows a mismatch. That confirms tampering, so you investigate and reinstall the file from its package.

A common mistake is keeping the baseline database writable on the same server. An attacker who gains root can simply update it. Keep a read-only or offsite copy instead.

The consequence for a running system: without these checks, a planted SUID shell or an altered system tool can give an attacker lasting root access that nobody notices. Integrity monitoring detects change but does not prevent it. You also need to refresh the baseline after legitimate updates, or the reports fill with noise.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm audits its file server for risky special permissions. Step 1: the admin runs find / -perm -4000 -type f to list every SUID file (SUID, or set-user-ID, is a special bit that makes a program run with its owner's privileges). Step 2: she compares the list with the programs she expects to see, such as /usr/bin/passwd and /usr/bin/sudo. Among them she finds /home/temp-clerk/.local/sh, a copy of a shell owned by root with mode 4755. Step 3: ____. Step 4: she removes the SUID bit from that file and starts investigating how it got there. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: She concludes it is low risk because SUID makes a program run with the privileges of whoever launches it, so nobody gains anything.
She concludes it is harmless because it sits in an ordinary user's home folder, not a system directory, so only that user can reach it.
She concludes it only matters if the file is also world-writable, so she reruns the search with find / -perm -0002 -type f first.
She flags it as serious: a root-owned SUID shell runs as root for anyone who starts it, so it could give lasting root access.
questions.why: SUID makes a program run with its owner's privileges, so a root-owned SUID shell gives root to anyone who runs it, which is exactly the planted backdoor these audits look for.

questions.prompt: On a print server, a script has the octal permissions 754. In octal notation each digit covers owner, group and others in that order, and read is worth 4, write 2 and execute 1. What can members of the file's group do with this script?
choices: Read it only
Write and execute it, but not read it
Read, write and execute it
Read and execute it, but not write to it
questions.why: The group digit is 5, which is read (4) plus execute (1), with no write (2).

questions.prompt: A charity runs a Debian-family Linux server and wants to check whether any installed system files no longer match the versions that came in their original packages. Which tool fits this job?
choices: aide --init
find / -perm -0002 -type f
debsums
rpm -Va
questions.why: debsums checks installed files against their original packages on Debian-family systems, while rpm -Va does the same job on Red Hat-family systems.

questions.prompt: A design studio set up AIDE, a file integrity monitoring tool that saves a baseline database of file hashes, owners, permissions and timestamps, and kept that database as a writable file on the same server. An attacker later got root and replaced /usr/bin/ls with a modified version, yet the next aide --check reported no changes. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The attacker, having root, updated the writable baseline so it matched the tampered file.
AIDE only reports permission changes and never compares file hashes.
Changing a file's contents does not change its SHA-256 hash, so AIDE could not see it.
AIDE blocks changes as they happen, so the change must have been reverted automatically.
questions.why: A writable baseline on the same server lets anyone with root rewrite it, so tampering disappears from reports, which is why the baseline should be kept read-only or offsite.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would audit a new server's file permissions and file integrity, and name at least one limit of these checks.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd do two passes. For permissions, I'd use find to list SUID and SGID files and world-writable files. SUID matters because a root-owned SUID program runs as root, so an unexpected one, like a shell copy in /tmp, is a classic backdoor. For integrity, right after install I'd build a baseline with a tool like AIDE. AIDE records each file's hash, owner, permissions and timestamps. Later I'd rerun it and look at what changed. A hash is a fingerprint of the contents, so any edit shows up. I can also use rpm -Va or debsums to compare files against their packages. The limits: this only detects tampering after it happens and doesn't block it. The baseline is only trustworthy if the system was clean when I built it and the database is stored where an attacker with root can't edit it. Legitimate updates also cause alerts unless I refresh the baseline.
rubricPoints: Explains owner, group and others permissions and why SUID or world-writable files are risky.
Describes using find to list SUID, SGID or world-writable files and comparing them with expectations.
Explains that a hash is a content fingerprint and that tools like AIDE compare against a known-good baseline.
Mentions package verification such as rpm -Va or debsums as another integrity check.
States that integrity monitoring detects rather than prevents change.
Notes that the baseline must be clean and protected from modification, and refreshed after legitimate updates.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner read and correct real file ownership and permission bits on a server, which is the hands-on core of permission auditing.

lessons.plain: SSH (Secure Shell) is the encrypted remote-login door into a Linux server. Hardening it means making that door harder to force. Two common steps are key-only login and blocking direct root login. With key-only login the server no longer accepts passwords. It accepts only someone holding a matching secret key file, much like a lock that opens for one physical key and ignores anyone who guesses combinations. Blocking root login means nobody can sign in straight as the all-powerful administrator account. People log in as themselves and raise their privileges only when they need to.
lessons.guessPrompt: Attackers on the internet try thousands of username and password guesses against a server's SSH door every day. If the server stopped accepting passwords completely and accepted only a secret key file kept on your laptop, what would those guessing attacks achieve?
lessons.teach:
SSH hardening means changing the SSH server's settings so remote logins are harder to steal or abuse. The SSH server program is called sshd, and it reads its settings from /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Some systems also read extra files from /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/.

Key-only authentication relies on a key pair, which is two linked files. The private key stays secret on your own machine. The public key is copied to the server into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the list of keys allowed to log in as that user. At login the server sends a challenge that only the matching private key can answer correctly. The private key itself never crosses the network. Setting PasswordAuthentication no tells sshd to refuse passwords entirely. A brute-force attack, meaning automated guessing of passwords, then has nothing to guess. Leaked or reused passwords also stop working against this server.

Disabling root login means setting PermitRootLogin no. Root is the superuser, the account that can do anything. Every Linux system has an account called root, so attackers already know half of the login. Blocking it forces people to log in as named users and then use sudo, a tool that lets a permitted user run a command with root rights. This also leaves a record of who did what.

Here is a worked example. First, on your laptop, run ssh-keygen to create a key pair. Second, run ssh-copy-id alice@server to place the public key in alice's authorized_keys. Third, open a new terminal and confirm that ssh alice@server logs in without asking for a password. Fourth, edit sshd_config to set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no. Fifth, check the file with sshd -t, then reload the service. Sixth, test a fresh login from a second session while the first session is still open.

The common mistake is turning off passwords before key login has been proven to work, or closing your only session before testing. On a remote server this locks you out, and the only way back in is the physical or cloud console. Note that these controls do not protect a private key that is stolen and has no passphrase.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's file server, files01, logs 4,000 failed logins overnight. Every attempt uses the username root with a different password. The admin, Priya, reasons it through. Step 1: These are automated password guesses, which is a brute-force attack. Step 2: The attacker picked root because every Linux system has that account, so half the login is already known. Step 3: ??? Step 4: After proving her own key login works, she sets PasswordAuthentication no, so no password guess can succeed for any account. Which choice is Step 3?
choices: Give root a much longer password so the guesses take more time to succeed.
Set PermitRootLogin no, so staff log in as named users and use sudo for root tasks.
Copy her private key into root's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys so root can use key login.
Delete the root account from files01 so that no attacker can target it at all.
questions.why: PermitRootLogin no blocks direct root logins, which removes the known target, and sudo from named accounts still lets permitted staff run root commands while recording who did what.

questions.prompt: A developer at a small shipping company logs in to a build server, using key-only authentication. What does her private key do during this login?
choices: It is sent to the server, which compares it against the copy stored in authorized_keys.
It is used to encrypt her password, and the server then checks that password.
It stays on her laptop and answers the server's challenge, and it is never sent over the network.
It is copied into the server's /etc/ssh/sshd_config so sshd can recognize her.
questions.why: In key-only login the server sends a challenge that only the matching private key can answer, and the private key itself never leaves the user's machine.

questions.prompt: Marco manages a remote server for a travel agency, and he has only one SSH session open. He sets PasswordAuthentication no, reloads sshd, and then closes that session. When he tries to log back in, his key is rejected because he had never actually copied it to the server. What is his situation?
choices: He can still log in with his password, because a reload only affects new users.
He can run ssh-copy-id from his laptop now to add the key, then log in normally.
He just has to wait for sshd to restart on its own, and passwords will work again.
He is locked out, and he must use the physical or cloud console to get back in.
questions.why: With passwords refused and no working key, SSH has no way left to let him in, so only console access can fix the settings.

questions.prompt: A university lab server uses key-only authentication and has PermitRootLogin no set. A researcher's laptop is stolen. Her private key on that laptop has no passphrase. What is true?
choices: The attacker can log in as the researcher, since these controls do not protect a stolen key without a passphrase.
The attacker cannot use the key, because private keys only work on the original laptop.
The attacker needs her password too, because key-only logins also ask for one.
The attacker cannot get in, because root login is disabled on the server.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that key-only authentication and disabling root login do not protect a private key that is stolen and has no passphrase, so whoever holds that key can log in as her.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you turned off SSH passwords and root login on the new server. Explain in your own words what each change defends against, and name one limit or tradeoff of these controls.
lessons.modelAnswer: I made two changes. First, I set the SSH server to accept keys only. Your private key stays on your machine and only the public key sits on the server. Login works by proving you hold the private key, so internet bots guessing passwords get nowhere, and a leaked password is useless here. Second, I blocked direct root login. Every Linux box has a root account, so attackers already know that username, and root can do anything. Now everyone logs in as themselves and uses sudo, which also leaves a trail of who ran what. There is a tradeoff. Keys move the risk to your laptop: a stolen private key with no passphrase still gets in, so protect your keys with passphrases. Losing your key can also lock you out. That's why I tested a new login in a second session before reloading sshd, and why we keep console access as a fallback.
rubricPoints: Key-only auth means the server checks possession of a private key whose public half sits in authorized_keys, and refuses passwords.
Disabling passwords defeats brute-force guessing and reuse of leaked passwords.
PermitRootLogin no removes the well-known all-powerful account as a login target and forces named users plus sudo for accountability.
Key login must be verified in a separate session before passwords are disabled and sshd is reloaded, to avoid lockout.
A limit: a stolen unprotected private key still grants access, so keys need passphrases and careful handling.

suggested.rationale: The skill is safely changing sshd settings in the right order and justifying each control. An exam-style scenario where the learner must sequence the steps and avoid a lockout teaches that best, since no listed mission has the learner edit the SSH configuration.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right secret, called a key, can turn it back into readable form. There are two moments when data needs that protection. At rest means data sitting on a disk: if someone steals the drive, they should see only noise. In transit means data moving across a network: if someone listens on the wire, they should see only noise. Think of a letter: locking it in a safe protects it while stored, and sealing it in a tamper-proof envelope protects it while posted. You need both, because each one covers a different moment.
lessons.guessPrompt: A laptop with an encrypted disk is stolen while it is switched on and logged in. Do you think the thief can read the files? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest protects stored data. On Linux the standard tool is LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup), a format for encrypting a whole disk partition. LUKS stores a random master key that actually encrypts the data. That master key is itself locked inside one or more keyslots. A keyslot is a copy of the master key protected by a passphrase or key file. This is why you can change a passphrase without re-encrypting the whole disk: only the keyslot changes. When you unlock the partition, the kernel maps it to a decrypted virtual device, and the system reads and writes through that device as normal.

Encryption in transit protects data moving between machines. TLS (Transport Layer Security) wraps connections such as HTTPS. The server proves its identity with a certificate, which is a signed document that ties a public key to a name. SSH (Secure Shell) does the same job for remote logins and file copies. It identifies the server by a host key that your client remembers after the first connection. Both protocols agree on a fresh session key, then encrypt and integrity-check every packet.

Here is a worked example. A database server keeps records on a LUKS partition, and clients connect over TLS. First, at boot an admin enters the passphrase, a keyslot releases the master key, and the partition unlocks. Second, a client connects, checks the server's certificate, and agrees on a session key. Third, a query travels encrypted over the network and is decrypted only at the server. Fourth, if someone later pulls the disk out of the powered-off server, they see only ciphertext, meaning scrambled bytes.

A common mistake is believing LUKS protects a running server. Once the partition is unlocked, any process or attacker with access to the live system reads plaintext. LUKS defends against stolen or discarded hardware, not against a compromised login. Likewise, TLS does nothing for data once it lands on disk. Using only one of the two leaves a gap.

questions.prompt: A surveyor at a mapping company carries a laptop whose data partition is encrypted with LUKS. Each evening she copies the day's 300 MB of survey files to the head-office server using SSH, a protocol for encrypted remote logins and file copies. Step 1: she powers on the laptop and types her passphrase; a keyslot releases the master key, and the partition unlocks into a decrypted virtual device. Step 2: missing. Step 3: the survey files travel across the hotel Wi-Fi as encrypted, integrity-checked packets and are decrypted only at the head-office server. Step 4: weeks later the powered-off laptop is stolen from her car, and the thief who reads the drive sees only ciphertext. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The server unlocks one of the laptop's keyslots with the surveyor's passphrase before accepting any files
Her laptop re-encrypts the whole partition with a new master key so the files are safe to send
Her SSH client checks the server's host key against the one it remembered from the first connection, then agrees on a fresh session key
Her laptop sends its LUKS master key to the server, so the server can decrypt the files as they arrive
questions.why: SSH identifies the server by a host key the client remembered earlier and then agrees on a fresh session key that encrypts every packet; LUKS keys never leave the laptop and play no part in protecting network traffic.

questions.prompt: A charity's file server has a 4 TB partition encrypted with LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup). After a volunteer leaves, the admin changes the unlock passphrase, and the change finishes in seconds. Why is it so quick?
choices: LUKS only encrypts new files, so the existing 4 TB never has to be touched
The passphrase encrypts the data directly, but LUKS caches the old result to save time
Only the keyslot holding a copy of the master key changes; the data stays encrypted under the same master key
The kernel's decrypted virtual device re-encrypts the data in the background after the change
questions.why: The data is encrypted by a random master key, and a passphrase only protects a keyslot copy of that key, so changing the passphrase rewrites just the keyslot.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's tracking server stores shipment records on a LUKS partition that was unlocked at boot. While the server is running, an attacker steals an admin's login and gets a shell on it. What can the attacker see in the shipment records?
choices: Only ciphertext, because LUKS keeps the records encrypted until the attacker supplies the passphrase
Nothing at all, because LUKS blocks logins from accounts that did not unlock the partition
Plaintext, because the unlocked partition is read through the decrypted virtual device like a normal disk
Only ciphertext, because the records are protected by the TLS session key while stored on disk
questions.why: Once a LUKS partition is unlocked, any process or attacker with access to the live system reads plaintext; LUKS defends against stolen or discarded hardware, not a compromised login.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's patient portal uses HTTPS, which wraps traffic in TLS (Transport Layer Security), and the server presents a valid certificate. Patient X-rays are saved on an unencrypted disk. The clinic later throws away an old drive from that server without wiping it. What is true about the X-rays on that drive?
choices: They are safe, because TLS encrypted them when they were uploaded and they stay encrypted on disk
They are unreadable, because the TLS session key is erased when the connection closes
They are exposed, because TLS only protects data in transit; protecting the stored files needs encryption at rest such as LUKS
They are safe, because the certificate ties the server's public key to its name and locks the stored files
questions.why: TLS encrypts data only while it moves over the network and does nothing once it lands on disk, so a discarded unencrypted drive leaves the X-rays readable; encryption at rest like LUKS closes that gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between encryption at rest and encryption in transit on a Linux server, which tools cover each, and one threat that each one does not stop.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk. On Linux that is usually LUKS, which encrypts a partition with a master key. The master key is guarded by passphrase keyslots, so you can change a passphrase without re-encrypting everything. Its job is to make a stolen or discarded drive unreadable. Its limit is that once the server is booted and the partition is unlocked, anyone who gets into the running system sees plaintext. So it does not stop a hacked account.

Encryption in transit protects data crossing the network. TLS does this for things like HTTPS, using certificates to prove the server's identity. SSH does it for remote logins and file copies, using host keys. Both stop eavesdropping and tampering on the wire. But they do nothing once data is written to disk, and they cannot help if you accept a fake certificate or host key. A server needs both kinds.
rubricPoints: Defines at rest as stored data and in transit as data moving over a network.
Names LUKS for disk encryption and TLS and SSH for network encryption.
Notes that LUKS only protects data while the volume is locked, for example a stolen or powered-off disk.
Notes that TLS and SSH protect only the connection, not the data after it lands on disk.
Mentions that trust depends on keys, such as a passphrase or keyslot, a certificate, or a host key.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about understanding which control covers which threat, so explaining the at-rest versus in-transit split and its limits is the core skill.

lessons.plain: A Bash script is a text file of the same commands you would type at a Linux prompt, saved so the computer can run them in order without you. It is like a written recipe: instead of remembering each step of a backup, you write the steps down once and reuse them. Four tools make a script smart rather than a fixed list. Variables are labelled boxes that hold values. Conditionals choose what to do based on a check. Loops repeat a step for many items. Functions give a group of steps a name so you can reuse them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A backup script contains the check `if [ -d /backup ]` before it copies files. What do you think that check is asking, and why might a script need to ask it before copying anything?
lessons.teach:
A Bash script is a plain text file of shell commands that Bash runs from top to bottom. Its first line, the shebang `#!/bin/bash`, tells the system which interpreter to use. Four building blocks turn a list of commands into a small program.

A variable is a named value. `DEST=/backup` stores text, and `$DEST` reads it back. There must be no spaces around the equals sign. Put reads in double quotes, `"$DEST"`, so a value containing spaces stays one piece.

A conditional runs commands only when something is true. Every command returns an exit status, a number where 0 means success and anything else means failure. `if` acts on that status: `if [ -d "$DEST" ]; then ... else ... fi`. The `[ ]` is the test command. `-d` asks whether a path is a directory, `-f` asks whether it is a regular file, and `-gt` compares numbers. `!` reverses the answer.

A loop repeats work. `for f in /var/log/*.log; do ... done` sets `f` to each matching filename in turn.

A function is a named, reusable block: `backup_one() { cp "$1" "$DEST"; }`. Inside it, `$1` is the first argument given when you call it, as in `backup_one app.log`.

Worked example. Suppose the script sets DEST=/backup, then runs `if [ ! -d "$DEST" ]; then mkdir "$DEST"; fi`, then `for f in /var/log/*.log; do backup_one "$f"; done`. Bash stores /backup in DEST. The test finds no such directory, `!` turns false into true, and mkdir runs. The pattern expands to, say, app.log and auth.log. On the first pass f is /var/log/app.log and the function copies it. The second pass copies auth.log.

A common mistake is writing `DEST = /backup` with spaces. Bash treats DEST as a command name, prints "command not found", and DEST stays empty. A later `rm -rf "$DEST"/*` would then expand to `rm -rf /*`. On a live server, an empty or misspelled variable can delete the wrong files. Careful scripts quote their variables, check that values are not empty, and often start with `set -u`, which stops the script when it uses an unset variable.

questions.prompt:
A small accounting firm uses this script to keep copies of monthly CSV reports.

KEEP=/srv/keep
if [ -d "$KEEP" ]; then echo "folder ready"; else mkdir "$KEEP"; fi
save() { cp "$1" "$KEEP"; }
for r in /srv/reports/*.csv; do save "$r"; done

Trace: (1) Bash stores /srv/keep in KEEP. (2) /srv/keep already exists, so the -d test is true. "folder ready" is printed and mkdir is skipped. (3) The pattern /srv/reports/*.csv expands to jan.csv, feb.csv and mar.csv. (4) On the first pass, r is /srv/reports/jan.csv, and the loop calls save with "$r". (5) ??? (6) The second and third passes do the same for feb.csv and mar.csv.

Which statement correctly fills in step 5?
choices: Inside save, $1 holds all three filenames at once, so all three are copied on this pass.
Inside save, $1 is /srv/keep, the destination folder, so cp copies the folder onto itself.
Inside save, $1 holds the letter r, because the loop variable is named r.
Inside save, $1 is /srv/reports/jan.csv, so cp copies jan.csv into /srv/keep.
questions.why: In a function, $1 is the first argument passed when the function is called, and the loop passes the current filename, so $1 is /srv/reports/jan.csv on this pass.

questions.prompt: A script line reads: if some_command; then echo yes; fi. How does the if statement decide whether to run echo?
choices: It checks whether some_command printed any text to the screen.
It compares the command's output to the word "yes".
It runs the then block only when the exit status is 1, because 1 means true.
It checks some_command's exit status: 0 means success, so the then block runs.
questions.why: Every command returns an exit status. if treats 0 as success and runs the then block, and any non-zero status counts as failure.

questions.prompt:
On a print server, the file /etc/printq.conf exists and is a regular file. A script runs:

CONF=/etc/printq.conf
if [ ! -f "$CONF" ]; then echo "missing"; else echo "found"; fi

What does the script print?
choices: Nothing, because -f only works on directories
An error, because ! cannot be used inside [ ]
found, because -f is true and ! reverses it to false
missing, because -f is true and the then block always runs first
questions.why: -f is true for an existing regular file, and ! reverses it to false, so the else branch runs and prints found.

questions.prompt:
A cleanup script for a school's lab machines contains these two lines:

TMPDIR = /var/tmp/labfiles
rm -rf "$TMPDIR"/*

What happens, and which change would make the script stop before any deletion?
choices: Bash stores the text "= /var/tmp/labfiles" in TMPDIR, so rm fails harmlessly. No change is needed.
Bash ignores the spaces and stores /var/tmp/labfiles, so the files in that folder are removed safely.
Bash tries to run TMPDIR as a command, TMPDIR stays empty, and rm targets /*. Starting the script with set -u makes it stop when it uses the unset variable.
The quotes around $TMPDIR stop rm from running at all when the variable is empty.
questions.why: Spaces around = make Bash treat TMPDIR as a command name, so the variable stays unset and the rm path expands to /*. set -u stops the script when it uses an unset variable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how variables, an if test, a for loop and a function work together in a short backup script. Name one way an unchecked variable can make such a script dangerous.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Bash script runs commands in order. I keep the destination in a variable, DEST=/backup, with no spaces around the equals sign, and I read it as "$DEST" in quotes so spaces in a path don't split it. Before copying, an if with the test command, [ -d "$DEST" ], checks that the folder exists. Every command returns an exit status, and 0 means true, so if the check fails I create the folder. A for loop then walks over each /var/log/*.log file. Each pass calls a function, backup_one, which copies whatever path it receives as $1. That keeps the copy logic in one place. The risk is that if DEST is misspelled or never set, it expands to nothing. A command like rm -rf "$DEST"/* would then target the root of the filesystem. So I check that variables are not empty, or use set -u to stop the script when a variable is unset.
rubricPoints: Variables are assigned with no spaces around = and read with $, ideally in double quotes.
if acts on exit status, where 0 means success, often through the [ ] test with flags like -d or -f.
A for loop assigns each item, such as each matching file, to a variable in turn.
A function is a named reusable block that receives arguments as $1, $2 and so on.
Names the risk that an empty or unset variable can make commands act on the wrong path, and gives a safeguard such as quoting, an emptiness check or set -u.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine has the learner write Bash. Tracing and explaining how a variable, test, loop and function combine is the closest way to check real understanding here.

lessons.plain: Scheduling means telling the computer to run a task for you at a set time, so nobody has to remember to type the command. Linux gives you three common tools. cron runs a task again and again on a repeating schedule, such as every night at 2:30. at runs a task once at a single future time, such as tonight at 11 pm. systemd timers also run tasks on a schedule, but they are managed by systemd, the program that starts and supervises services. Think of cron as a weekly alarm clock, at as a one-off kitchen timer, and systemd timers as an alarm clock that also writes a logbook.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need a backup script to run every Monday at 2:30 in the morning, and separately you need to restart a service just once tonight at 11 pm. Would you use the same scheduling tool for both jobs, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
cron is a background service, called a daemon, that reads crontabs. A crontab is a table of scheduled jobs. Each user edits their own with crontab -e and lists it with crontab -l. Each line has five time fields, then the command. In order, the fields are minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12) and day of week (0-7, where both 0 and 7 mean Sunday). An asterisk means every value. The system-wide file /etc/crontab adds a sixth field naming the user the job runs as.

Worked example: 30 2 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh. Read it left to right. Minute is 30 and hour is 2, so the job runs at 02:30. Day of month is *, so any date. Month is *, so any month. Day of week is 1, so Monday. The result is that the backup runs every Monday at 02:30.

at runs a command once. For example, typing at 23:00 and then entering a command queues it for 11 pm. atq lists the waiting jobs and atrm removes one. at needs its own daemon, atd, to be running.

A systemd timer is a unit file ending in .timer. A unit file is a configuration file that systemd manages. The timer starts a matching .service unit, which holds the actual command. The setting OnCalendar gives a calendar time, such as Mon 02:30. OnBootSec gives a delay counted from boot. Persistent=true makes the timer run a job it missed because the machine was off. Plain cron simply skips missed runs. You can see the next run times with systemctl list-timers, and the job's output goes to the journal, the systemd log.

Common mistake: writing a cron job that works in your terminal but fails under cron. Cron starts jobs with a very small environment. Its PATH, the list of folders searched for commands, is short, so a command that is not in those folders cannot be found. In a running system the backup silently never happens. Use full paths, and send output to a log file so failures are visible.

questions.prompt: A small bakery chain wants its cleanup script to run on a schedule. The admin adds this line to their own crontab: 45 4 * 7 0 /srv/tools/clean.sh. Read it left to right. Step 1: Minute is 45 and hour is 4, so the time is 04:45. Step 2: Day of month is *, so any date. Step 3: Month is 7, so July only. Step 4: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Day of week is 0, which means every day, so the job runs at 04:45 every day in July.
Day of week is 0, which means Sunday, so the job runs at 04:45 on every Sunday in July.
Day of week is 0, which is not allowed because days of the week run from 1 to 7, so cron rejects the line.
Day of week is 0, which means Monday because the week starts counting at 0, so it runs on July Mondays.
questions.why: In cron's day-of-week field both 0 and 7 mean Sunday, so the line runs at 04:45 on every Sunday in July.

questions.prompt: A technician at a dental clinic needs a database service restarted exactly once, tonight at 21:00, and never again. Which approach fits best?
choices: Create a systemd timer with OnBootSec set so it fires after the next boot.
Add a line to /etc/crontab with a sixth field naming the root user.
Add a line to their crontab with minute 0 and hour 21 and leave it in place.
Use at 21:00 to queue the command once, making sure the atd daemon is running.
questions.why: at runs a command a single time at the given time, and it needs its daemon, atd, running; cron and timers are built for repeated schedules.

questions.prompt: At a logistics firm, a script called sync.sh runs perfectly when an admin types it in a terminal. Scheduled through cron, the expected files never appear and no error is shown anywhere. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Cron skips jobs that print output, so remove every echo line from the script.
Cron starts jobs with a very short PATH, so commands are not found; use full paths and send output to a log file.
Cron only runs scripts on Sundays unless the day-of-week field is set to 7, so change that field.
The crontab must be listed with crontab -l before cron will load it, so run that command once.
questions.why: Cron gives jobs a tiny environment with a short PATH, so commands outside those folders fail silently unless you use full paths and log the output.

questions.prompt: A design studio's workstation is switched off every night. A systemd timer with OnCalendar=Sat 01:00 runs a weekly archive job, but the archive never happens because the machine is off at that time. What setting makes the job run after the machine is next turned on?
choices: Add Persistent=true to the timer so a run missed while the machine was off is carried out.
Move the job into a plain cron entry, since cron catches up on missed runs automatically.
Put the command in the .timer file instead of the .service file so it starts sooner.
Replace OnCalendar with atq so the job waits in the queue until power returns.
questions.why: Persistent=true tells the timer to run a job it missed because the machine was off, whereas plain cron simply skips missed runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between cron, at and a systemd timer for a nightly backup script, including one limit or tradeoff of the option you do not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a nightly backup I need a repeating schedule, so at is out, because it only runs a job once. Cron is the quickest choice. I add one crontab line, such as 30 2 * * * with the script's full path, because cron gives jobs a minimal environment and a short PATH. The weakness of cron is that if the server is off at 02:30, that night's backup is skipped. Its output also goes nowhere useful unless I redirect it to a log. A systemd timer takes more setup: a .timer file plus a .service file. In return, Persistent=true catches up on missed runs, systemctl list-timers shows when it will run next, and the journal keeps its output. For a backup on a machine that may be powered off, I would pick the timer. On an always-on server, cron is fine.
rubricPoints: Says cron and systemd timers handle repeating jobs while at handles a one-time job.
Reads or writes the five cron time fields in the correct order.
Explains that a systemd timer triggers a matching service unit and can catch up on missed runs with Persistent=true.
Notes that cron's minimal environment means scripts need full paths and logged output.
Names a real tradeoff such as setup effort versus missed runs and logging.

suggested.rationale: The mission has the learner find and read real crontab entries on a server, which practises decoding cron schedules and seeing what a scheduled job actually runs.

lessons.plain: A regular expression, or regex, is a small pattern that describes what a piece of text looks like rather than spelling it out exactly. Think of it as a stencil: you hold it over every line of a log file and keep the lines whose shape fits. Linux has three classic tools that use these patterns. grep finds the matching lines. sed edits text as it streams past, often swapping one thing for another. awk splits each line into columns so you can pull out or count the parts you care about. Together they let an admin turn thousands of log lines into a short, useful answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: You want only the log lines that begin with the word ERROR, not lines that merely mention an error somewhere in the middle. What extra detail would your search need to express besides the word itself?
lessons.teach:
A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that describes a set of text strings. Linux text tools read input one line at a time and test each line against the pattern. grep prints the lines that match. sed (the stream editor) changes lines as they pass through, most often with substitution in the form s/pattern/replacement/. awk splits each line into fields, by default on spaces, named $1, $2 and so on, and runs an action on each line or only on the lines that match a pattern.

A few symbols do most of the work. ^ ties a match to the start of a line, and $ ties it to the end. A dot matches any single character. [0-9] is a character class, meaning any one character from that set. * means zero or more of the item before it. In extended regex, turned on with grep -E or sed -E, + means one or more, ? means optional, | means or, and parentheses group text so it can be reused. A backslash makes a special character literal, so \. matches a real dot. This works because the matching engine slides along each line looking for any position where the whole pattern fits. You describe the shape of the text, not its exact contents.

Worked example. A line reads: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 22. Step 1: grep 'Failed password' auth.log keeps only failed-login lines. Step 2: pipe the result to awk '{print $6}'. Counting the fields gives Failed=1, password=2, for=3, root=4, from=5, and the IP address=6, so awk prints the address. Step 3: sort | uniq -c counts how often each address appears. Another way to do step 2 is sed -E 's/.*from ([0-9.]+) .*/\1/'. The parentheses capture the address, and \1 replaces the whole line with only that captured text.

Common mistakes: leaving patterns unquoted, so the shell expands * into filenames before grep ever sees the pattern, and forgetting that a dot is special, so 10.0.0.1 also matches 10x0y0z1. Field numbers are another trap. A line like Failed password for invalid user bob has extra words, so $6 is no longer the IP address. In an automated alert or cleanup script, a loose pattern quietly acts on the wrong lines.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's disk monitor writes lines like this to disk.log: 2024-05-03 14:02:11 disk /dev/sdb usage 91%. An admin wants to know which devices most often run above 90% full. Step 1: grep 'usage 9[0-9]%' disk.log keeps only lines where usage is between 90% and 99%. Step 2: ______ prints just the device name from each kept line. Step 3: sort | uniq -c counts how often each device appears. Which command belongs in Step 2?
choices: awk '{print $5}'
awk '{print $4}'
awk '{print $0}'
awk '{print $3}'
questions.why: Splitting on spaces gives date=1, time=2, disk=3, /dev/sdb=4, usage=5, 91%=6, so the device name is field $4.

questions.prompt: An application log at a dental clinic has many lines that mention the word timeout. You want grep to show only the lines whose last word is timeout. Which command does that?
choices: grep 'timeout$' app.log
grep 'timeout*' app.log
grep '^timeout' app.log
grep '.timeout' app.log
questions.why: The $ ties the match to the end of the line, so only lines that end in timeout match.

questions.prompt: A cleanup script at a school runs grep '172.16.5.4' firewall.log to find one specific host. Which of these lines would it also match, even though it is not that address?
choices: 172-16-5-4 rejected
172.16.54 accepted
172.16.5 accepted
17216.5.4 accepted
questions.why: An unescaped dot matches any single character, so each dash fits where a dot sits in the pattern. Writing \. would match only a real dot.

questions.prompt: A storage report at a design studio contains the line: user=maria quota=500MB used=320MB. What does sed -E 's/.*quota=([0-9]+)MB.*/\1/' print for this line?
choices: quota=500MB
user=maria 500
500MB
questions.why: The parentheses capture only the digits after quota=. Because the pattern covers the whole line, \1 replaces the whole line with just 500.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use grep, sed and awk with a regular expression to pull the offending IP addresses out of an auth log. Include one limit or tradeoff of relying on a fixed awk field number or a loose pattern.
lessons.modelAnswer: A regex is a pattern describing the shape of text, and the tools test each line against it. First I'd run grep 'Failed password' on the log so only the failed-login lines are left. Then I'd use awk to print the field that holds the IP. awk splits on spaces, so I count the words to find the right column. Finally I'd pipe to sort and uniq -c to count attempts per address. Instead of awk, sed -E with a capture group like ([0-9.]+) after 'from' can keep only the address. The tradeoff is fragility. A fixed field number breaks when the line format changes, for example when 'invalid user' adds words. A loose pattern, such as an unescaped dot, can match lines I didn't intend. I'd quote every pattern, escape literal dots, anchor with ^ or $ where it helps, and check the output on sample lines before trusting it in a script.
rubricPoints: Defines a regex as a pattern describing the shape of text, tested line by line.
States the role of each tool: grep filters lines, sed substitutes or edits, awk splits lines into fields.
Uses at least one regex element correctly, such as an anchor, character class, quantifier or capture group.
Walks through a concrete pipeline from raw log lines to a counted result.
Names a limit, such as shifting field positions, unescaped dots or unquoted patterns matching the wrong text.

suggested.rationale: Investigating failed SSH logins makes the learner filter auth logs with grep and extract and count IP addresses with awk or sed, which is exactly this skill.

lessons.plain: Version control is a system that keeps a dated, labeled history of every change made to a set of files, so you can see who changed what, when, and why, and go back to any earlier version. Git is the most common version control tool. For an admin, the files are often scripts and configuration files. Think of it like the save points in a video game. Each time things work, you make a save point with a note. If a later change breaks the server, you load the last good save point instead of trying to remember what you edited.
lessons.guessPrompt: You edit a working backup script on Friday, and on Monday it fails. What would you most want to have recorded about Friday's edit to fix it quickly?
lessons.teach:
Git is a version control tool that records snapshots of files over time. A repository (repo) is a folder whose history Git tracks, stored in a hidden .git directory. You create one with git init, or copy an existing one with git clone. The working tree is the files as you are editing them right now. The staging area is a holding list of the changes you have chosen to include in the next snapshot, filled with git add. A commit is a saved snapshot with an author, a time, a unique ID (a hash), and a message, made with git commit -m "message". git status shows what changed and what is staged. git diff shows the exact lines changed. git log lists past commits. git revert makes a new commit that undoes an earlier one, so history is kept. A branch is a separate line of commits for trying changes safely. A remote is a shared copy on another server, updated with git push and fetched with git pull.

This works because every commit is a full, labeled restore point, and the history explains each change.

Worked example: in /opt/scripts you run git init. You git add backup.sh and commit with "initial working backup". Next you change the destination path. git diff shows the one changed line. You git add backup.sh and commit "move backups to /srv/backup". On Monday the backup fails. git log shows the second commit, and git revert with its hash restores the old path while recording that you did so.

Common mistake: committing secrets such as passwords or keys inside scripts or config files. Once committed, a secret stays in the history even after you delete the file, and anyone who clones the repo can read it. List such files in a .gitignore file, which tells Git never to track them, and keep the secrets elsewhere.

In a running system, version-controlled configs mean a bad change can be found and rolled back in minutes instead of rebuilt from memory.

questions.prompt: At a small veterinary clinic, an admin keeps a nightly sync script, sync_records.sh, in /srv/clinic-tools. The script reads a database password from a separate file called db.env. The team wants the scripts shared on a remote server so two other admins can clone them, but the password must never end up in Git's history. The plan so far: (1) run git init in /srv/clinic-tools. (2) ______ (3) git add sync_records.sh and the .gitignore file. (4) git commit -m "add nightly records sync". (5) git push to the shared remote. Which action belongs in step 2?
choices: Run git add db.env so the password file is backed up along with the script
Create a .gitignore file that lists db.env, so Git never tracks it
Put the password in the commit message instead of in db.env
Commit db.env now and delete it in a later commit before anyone clones the repo
questions.why: A .gitignore entry tells Git never to track db.env, so the secret stays out of every commit and out of every clone, while the password itself is kept elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A technician at a logistics company has edited three files in a Git repo: haproxy.cfg, firewall.rules and notes.txt. She wants only haproxy.cfg and firewall.rules in the next commit. What does running git add on just those two files do?
choices: It undoes the changes to notes.txt so it cannot be committed
It immediately saves a permanent snapshot of those two files with a hash
It puts those two changes in the staging area, the list of what the next commit will include
It uploads those two files to the shared remote server
questions.why: git add fills the staging area with the chosen changes; nothing becomes a snapshot until git commit runs, and notes.txt stays edited but unstaged.

questions.prompt: A colleague at a university IT office changed timeout values in a version-controlled file called proxy.conf but has not committed yet. Before you approve the change, you want to see exactly which lines were altered. Which command shows that?
choices: git commit -m "review", because a commit records the changes
git status, because it shows which files changed
git log, because it lists every past commit
git diff, because it shows the exact lines changed
questions.why: git diff shows the exact lines changed; git status only names the changed files and whether they are staged, and git log only lists commits already made.

questions.prompt: At a print shop, an admin accidentally committed api_keys.conf containing a live API key. Two commits later, he deleted the file and committed that deletion. The repo is on a remote that four contractors can clone. What is the situation now?
choices: The key is safe, because deleting the file in a new commit removes it from all of history
The key is safe as long as nobody runs git pull again
The key is safe, because contractors only receive the current working tree when they clone
The key is still exposed, because the earlier commit with the file stays in the history that anyone who clones can read
questions.why: Every commit is a full, kept snapshot, so a committed secret remains in the history after deletion, and anyone who clones the repo can read it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why we should keep our admin scripts and config files in git, how a change goes from edit to commit, and one limit or risk of using git this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Git keeps a history of our scripts and configs as a series of commits, which are labeled snapshots with an author, a time, and a message saying why. When I change a file in the working tree, I check it with git status and git diff, choose what to include with git add, which puts it in the staging area, then save it with git commit and a clear message. If a change breaks something, git log helps find the commit, and git revert undoes it with a new commit so the history stays honest. We can push to a shared remote so everyone has the same versions. The limit is that git only remembers what we commit: uncommitted edits are not protected. The big risk is secrets. If a password gets committed it stays in history, so we keep secret files out with .gitignore.
rubricPoints: Defines a commit as a labeled snapshot with author, time and message.
Describes the edit, add to staging, commit flow.
Explains rollback using log and revert to a known-good version.
Mentions sharing through a remote with push and pull.
Names a limit or risk such as uncommitted changes being unprotected or secrets persisting in history.

suggested.rationale: Rolling back a bad release to a known-good version is the practical payoff of keeping a commit history, so doing it makes the value of version control concrete.

lessons.plain: Configuration management means describing how your servers should be set up (which software is installed, which settings files contain what, which services are running) and letting a tool make every server match that description. Infrastructure as code means keeping that description in plain text files, so it can be reviewed, versioned and reused like any program. Think of a recipe card versus cooking from memory: with the card, every cook makes the same dish, and if a dish comes out wrong you compare it to the card. Ansible is one popular tool of this kind. It connects to servers over the network and brings each one into line with the written description.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a written instruction that says 'make sure the web server package is installed and running' and you apply it to a server where it is already installed and running. What do you think a well-designed tool should do the second time, and why?
lessons.teach:
Configuration management (CM) is the practice of defining the desired state of systems (packages, files, users, services) and automatically enforcing it. Infrastructure as code (IaC) is storing that definition in text files kept under version control, so changes are reviewed and repeatable instead of typed by hand.

Most CM tools are declarative: you state what the end result should be, not the step-by-step commands. A script that runs 'install package, then start service' is imperative. The tool works out what, if anything, needs changing. This makes tasks idempotent, meaning running them once or ten times gives the same result, and a second run changes nothing.

Ansible vocabulary: an inventory is the list of hosts (servers) to manage, often grouped, such as 'web' or 'db'. A playbook is a YAML file (a readable, indentation-based text format) listing tasks to apply to hosts. Each task calls a module, a small built-in unit that knows how to check and set one kind of thing, such as a package or a service. Ansible is agentless: it pushes changes over SSH from a control machine, with no extra software installed on the targets. Some other tools use an agent on each server that pulls its configuration from a central server.

Worked example: a playbook says the web group should have nginx installed and the nginx service running. The inventory lists web1, web2 and web3. On the first run, web1 already has nginx running, so it reports 'ok'. web2 lacks the package, so it is installed and started, reporting 'changed'. web3 has nginx installed but stopped, so it is only started. On the second run, all three report 'ok' and nothing is touched.

A common mistake is wrapping raw shell commands in tasks, such as appending a line to a config file with echo. That is not idempotent, so every run adds another copy of the line. In a running system, this builds up duplicate settings, and the server slowly drifts away from what the file describes. Drift means the real state no longer matches the defined state, and declarative modules exist to detect and correct it.

questions.prompt:
A clinic's IT team manages three database servers, listed in an inventory group called 'db': db-a, db-b and db-c. Their playbook declares that each server should have the postgresql package installed and a user account named 'pgadmin' present. Each task uses a module, the built-in unit that checks and sets one kind of thing.

First run: db-a already has postgresql and the pgadmin user, so both tasks report 'ok'. db-b has postgresql but no pgadmin user, so the user is created and that task reports 'changed'. db-c has neither, so the package is installed and the user is created, and both tasks report 'changed'.

Second run, with nobody touching the servers in between: db-a reports 'ok' and db-b reports 'ok'. What does db-c report on this second run?
choices: 'ok' for both tasks, and nothing on db-c is touched
'failed' for the user task, because the pgadmin account already exists
'changed' for both tasks, because db-c was changed on the previous run
'changed' for the package task only, because the module reinstalls it to confirm it works
questions.why: Declarative modules are idempotent: they check the current state, find db-c already matches the desired state, and change nothing, so both tasks report 'ok'.

questions.prompt: A team at a logistics company writes two versions of the same automation. Version A is a script that runs 'add the user deploy', then 'create the folder /srv/app', then 'copy the config file'. Version B is a file that states 'the user deploy exists, the folder /srv/app exists, and the config file has this content'. Which description is correct?
choices: Both are declarative, because both are saved as text files
Both are imperative, because both eventually make changes on the server
Version A is imperative and Version B is declarative
Version A is declarative and Version B is imperative
questions.why: Imperative means listing step-by-step commands (Version A), while declarative means stating the end result and letting the tool work out what needs changing (Version B).

questions.prompt: A university wants to manage 40 lab servers with Ansible from one admin laptop, and it does not want to install any extra management software on the lab servers. Why does Ansible fit this requirement?
choices: Ansible installs a small agent on each server that pulls its configuration from the laptop
Ansible only works when the servers are listed in a YAML playbook instead of an inventory
Ansible requires each server to run a central server that the laptop connects to
Ansible is agentless: it pushes changes over SSH from a control machine, so the targets need no extra software
questions.why: Ansible pushes changes over SSH from a control machine with no software installed on the targets, unlike agent-based tools where each server pulls its configuration.

questions.prompt: A retailer's playbook includes a task that runs a raw shell command to append the line 'MaxSessions 10' to the SSH configuration file using echo. The playbook is run on a schedule, five times in total. What is the most likely result on the server?
choices: The line appears once, because Ansible detects that it is already there
The task fails on the second run because the file has already been edited
The line appears five times, and the server drifts from what the configuration definition describes
The line is removed on the second run and re-added on the third
questions.why: A raw echo append is not idempotent, so every run adds another copy, building up duplicate settings and causing drift between the real state and the defined state.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who still fixes servers by logging in and typing commands why the team should describe server setup as declarative, idempotent code in a tool like Ansible. Include one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Instead of logging into each server and typing commands, we write down the state we want, for example 'nginx installed and running, this config file present'. We keep that in a playbook under version control. Ansible reads an inventory of hosts, connects over SSH without needing an agent, and uses modules that check each item first and change only what differs. Because the tasks are idempotent, we can run them again safely: servers already correct report 'ok', and servers that have drifted get fixed. Every change is reviewable, and new servers come out identical. The tradeoff is up-front effort and discipline. Someone has to learn the tool and write the definitions. If people still make manual changes, those get overwritten or cause drift. And if you fall back on raw shell commands inside tasks, you lose idempotency, so a repeated run can do harm, such as adding duplicate config lines.
rubricPoints: Defines configuration management as defining and enforcing a desired state across systems.
Explains infrastructure as code as keeping that definition in versioned text files.
Contrasts declarative (what) with imperative (how) steps.
Explains idempotency: repeated runs change nothing once the state is correct.
Uses Ansible terms correctly: inventory, playbook, module, agentless push over SSH.
Names a real limit, such as learning effort, manual changes causing drift, or non-idempotent shell tasks.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs a configuration management tool, and this objective is conceptual, so explaining declarative, idempotent desired state in your own words is the core skill to practice.

lessons.plain: A container is a way to package a program together with everything it needs to run (its libraries, settings and files) so it behaves the same on any Linux machine. Think of a shipping container: the crane does not care what is inside, it just moves a standard box. Unlike a full virtual machine, a container does not carry its own operating system kernel. It shares the host's kernel and is simply walled off from other programs. That makes it fast to start and light on memory. Docker is the most common tool for building, starting and listing containers.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a recipe card is the instructions and a cooked meal is the result, which one do you think a Docker image is, and which one is a running container? Can you cook several meals from one card?
lessons.teach:
A container is an isolated process, or group of processes, on a Linux host. The kernel (the core of the operating system that manages hardware and processes) gives it its own view of files, process IDs and network using namespaces, which are kernel features that hide everything else from the process. It also limits the CPU and memory it can use with cgroups (control groups). Because the kernel is shared, a container starts in seconds and uses far less memory than a virtual machine, which boots a whole operating system of its own.

An image is the read-only template a container starts from: a stack of file layers plus default settings. A container is one running (or stopped) instance of an image. One image can start many containers. A registry is a server that stores images for download. Docker Hub is the public default.

Three basic Docker commands. docker run starts a new container from an image, downloading the image first if it is missing. docker ps lists containers. docker images lists the images stored locally.

Worked example: type docker run -d --name web nginx. Docker looks for an image called nginx locally, finds none, and pulls it from the registry. It creates a container named web and starts it detached (-d, meaning in the background). Next, docker images shows nginx with its tag (a version label, latest by default) and size. Then docker ps shows web, its container ID (a short unique identifier), its image and the status Up.

Common mistake: deciding a container vanished because docker ps does not show it. By default docker ps lists only running containers. A container that exited is still there, and docker ps -a shows it. A related trap is assuming files written inside a container are permanent. They live in that container's writable layer and are lost when the container is removed, unless they are stored on a volume (storage mounted from outside the container).

questions.prompt: At a small public library, an admin types docker run -d --name catalog redis on a server that has never used Docker before. Trace what happens. Step 1: Docker looks for an image called redis in local storage and finds none. Step 2: ______. Step 3: Docker creates a container named catalog from that image and starts it detached, meaning in the background. Step 4: docker images now lists redis with its tag (latest, because none was given) and its size. Step 5: docker ps lists catalog with its container ID, the image redis and the status Up. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Docker stops with an error, because an image must be created by hand before docker run can use it
Docker boots a small virtual machine with its own operating system so that redis has a kernel to run on
Docker downloads (pulls) the redis image from a registry, which by default is Docker Hub
Docker creates an empty container named catalog and fills it with redis files later, once the container is Up
questions.why: When the requested image is missing locally, docker run first pulls it from a registry (Docker Hub by default), and only then creates and starts the container.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a reporting container on a shared Linux server. The team wants to make sure that this container can never use more than 2 GB of the server's memory. Which kernel feature limits a container's CPU and memory use?
choices: Namespaces
A registry
The image's read-only layers
cgroups (control groups)
questions.why: Cgroups limit how much CPU and memory a container can use, while namespaces only control what the container can see.

questions.prompt: A developer at a travel agency starts three containers from the same httpd image, naming them site-a, site-b and site-c. All three are running. No other images or containers exist on the host. What will docker images and docker ps show?
choices: docker images shows three httpd entries, and docker ps shows three containers
docker images shows one httpd entry, and docker ps shows one container, because containers from the same image are merged
docker images shows one httpd entry, and docker ps shows three containers
docker images shows nothing, because the image is in use, and docker ps shows three containers
questions.why: One image can start many containers, so the single locally stored httpd image is listed once, and each of the three running containers is listed separately.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, a container named backup-job ran a nightly task and then finished. The next morning a technician runs docker ps, sees no backup-job, and concludes that the container was deleted. What is the best next step?
choices: Run docker ps -a, because plain docker ps lists only running containers and an exited container is still there
Run docker run again with the same name, because that will show the old container's status
Run docker images, because exited containers move to the image list
Accept that it is gone, because containers are removed automatically when they stop
questions.why: By default docker ps shows only running containers, and docker ps -a also lists stopped or exited ones, so backup-job would appear there.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a container is, how it differs from an image and from a virtual machine, and what docker run, docker ps and docker images each do. Include one limit or tradeoff of containers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container is an isolated process on a Linux host. Namespaces give it its own view of files, process IDs and network, and cgroups cap its CPU and memory. It starts from an image, which is a read-only template of file layers and settings. The image is like a recipe, and each container is one meal made from it, so one image can run many containers. Unlike a virtual machine, a container shares the host's kernel, so it starts fast and uses little memory. docker run creates and starts a container, pulling the image from a registry if needed. docker ps lists running containers, and -a adds stopped ones. docker images lists local images. Tradeoffs: shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a VM's, and a container can't run a different OS kernel. Data written inside a container is lost when it is removed unless you use a volume.
rubricPoints: A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel, using namespaces and cgroups.
An image is a read-only template, and a container is a running or stopped instance of it.
Containers are lighter and faster than virtual machines because they do not boot their own OS.
docker run starts a container and pulls a missing image, docker ps lists containers, docker images lists local images.
docker ps hides stopped containers unless you add -a.
Names a limit, such as weaker isolation than a VM or data loss without a volume.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs Docker, and the core skill at this level is clearly explaining the image, container and VM distinction alongside what the three commands show.

scenarios.title: The Inherited Web Server at Brightmoor Bakeries
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightmoor Bakeries, a fictional regional bakery chain, as a junior systems engineer. The previous administrator left without notes, and you have been handed SSH access (a secure remote command-line login) to a Linux server called orders01. It runs the online ordering website. Customers report the site is down this morning. You have no graphical desktop, only a shell (the text prompt where you type commands).

Your manager gives you a few facts. The file /etc/os-release, a plain text file that names the Linux distribution (the specific flavour of Linux, such as Ubuntu or Rocky Linux), says ID_LIKE="rhel fedora". That means orders01 belongs to the Red Hat family. The website is served by nginx, a web server program. Software on Linux is installed as packages, which are bundles of program files plus information about what they need. A package manager is the tool that installs, removes and lists those packages. Red Hat family systems use dnf (older ones use yum) as the main package manager, with rpm as the lower-level tool underneath. Debian family systems use apt and dpkg instead.

Background programs such as nginx run as services, also called daemons. On this server they are controlled by systemd, the first program the kernel starts at boot. systemd starts and supervises everything else. systemd describes each service in a unit (a small configuration file, for example nginx.service). Its logging part, the journal, records what each unit printed.

Storage on orders01 uses LVM (Logical Volume Manager). LVM is a layer that pools one or more disk partitions, called physical volumes, into a volume group. It then carves that group into flexible virtual disks called logical volumes. A filesystem, which is the structure that organises files on a disk (for example xfs or ext4), sits on a logical volume. It becomes reachable once it is mounted, meaning attached to a directory called a mount point, such as /var/www. The file /etc/fstab lists the filesystems that should be mounted automatically at boot.

Using only command-line tools, complete these tasks:
1. Confirm whether the nginx package is installed on orders01, and show how you would install it if it were missing. Also state what the equivalent check would be on a Debian-family system.
2. Find out whether the nginx service is running and whether it is set to start at boot. Show how to read its recent log messages, then start it now and make it start automatically on every boot.
3. The website files live under /var/www. Describe how you would see the server's disk and LVM layout and confirm whether /var/www is actually mounted and how full it is. Say which file you would check to see whether it is supposed to mount at boot.
subParts: Check and install the nginx package
Inspect, troubleshoot and enable the nginx service
Inspect storage layout and the /var/www mount
modelAnswer: Because orders01 is Red Hat family, query the package database. Running rpm -q nginx prints the installed version (for example nginx-1.x.x), or it reports that the package is not installed. Running dnf list installed nginx gives the same answer through the higher-level tool. If nginx is missing, install it with sudo dnf install nginx. sudo runs the command with administrator rights, and dnf also pulls in any packages nginx depends on. On a Debian-family system you would check with dpkg -l nginx or apt list --installed nginx, and install with sudo apt install nginx. A common mistake is using the wrong family's tool, for example typing apt on a Red Hat system. The command will not exist or will do nothing useful.

Run systemctl status nginx. It shows whether the unit is active (running), inactive or failed, plus the last few log lines. Run systemctl is-enabled nginx to see whether it is enabled, meaning set to start at boot. To read its fuller recent logs, run journalctl -u nginx. The -u option limits output to that one unit. Adding -e jumps to the end and -b limits output to the current boot. Look there for errors, such as a bad configuration file or a port already in use, before restarting. Start it now with sudo systemctl start nginx. Make it start on every boot with sudo systemctl enable nginx, or do both at once with sudo systemctl enable --now nginx. Then confirm again with systemctl status nginx. A common mistake is running only start. The site then works until the next reboot and goes down again, because the service was never enabled.

Run lsblk to see the disks, their partitions and the logical volumes on them as a tree, with each mount point shown. For the LVM layers, run pvs to list physical volumes, vgs for volume groups and lvs for logical volumes. Run findmnt /var/www, or mount | grep /var/www, to confirm whether a filesystem is currently mounted there and which device it comes from. Run df -h /var/www to show its size, used and free space in human-readable units. A full filesystem can itself stop a web server writing logs or files.
