Check /etc/fstab to see whether /var/www has an entry that should mount it at boot. A common mistake is checking only that the /var/www directory exists. An unmounted mount point is still an ordinary, often empty, directory. nginx may then serve nothing or the wrong files even though the path looks fine.

scenarios.title: Setting Up a Shared Accounting Folder at Fernhill Bakery Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You are the new junior Linux administrator at Fernhill Bakery Supply, a fictional wholesale bakery distributor. The company keeps its invoices on a Linux server called ledger01. A new accountant, Priya Nair, starts on Monday. Your team lead has left you a note with four tasks.

Some background terms first. A user account is a login identity on the server, with its own name, ID number, and usually a home directory (a personal folder such as /home/priya). A group is a named set of users that can be given access to files as a unit. Every user has one primary group, the group that normally owns the files they create. They can also belong to extra groups, called supplementary groups. On ledger01 a group called accounting already exists, and its members are the accountants.

Every file and directory has an owner (a user), a group owner, and three sets of permissions: one for the owner, one for the group, and one for everyone else (others). Each set can include r (read), w (write, meaning change or add and remove entries), and x (execute, which for a directory means you can enter it). Permissions are often written as numbers: r=4, w=2, x=1, added together per set. So 7 means rwx, 6 means rw-, and 0 means no access at all. A fourth digit placed in front holds special bits. The SGID bit (value 2) on a directory makes new files inside it take the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group. The sticky bit (value 1) on a directory means only a file's owner, the directory's owner, or root can delete or rename that file. Root is the all-powerful administrator account.

The umask is a per-user setting that removes permissions from new files and directories at the moment they are created. Linux starts new files at 666 (rw for everyone) and new directories at 777, then switches off any bit that is set in the umask. With a umask of 022, new files come out as 644 and new directories as 755.

SSH (Secure Shell) is an encrypted remote-login service. On the server it is provided by a daemon, which is a background program, called sshd. Its settings live in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Background services like this are managed with systemctl, the control command for systemd, which is the service manager on most modern Linux systems.

The note says:

"Priya needs a login with a home directory and a bash shell, and she must be in the accounting group. Last month someone added a user to a group and the user accidentally lost all their other group memberships, so be careful. The shared folder /srv/accounts has to be usable by all accountants and by nobody else. Right now, files people save there end up owned by their personal groups, so colleagues can't open them, and once someone deleted a coworker's spreadsheet by mistake. Even when the group is right, new files are created as 644, so teammates can read them but can't edit them. Finally, Priya will work remotely over SSH. Make sure the SSH service runs now and after reboots, and stop anyone logging in directly as root over SSH."

1. Give the commands to create Priya's account (username priya) with a home directory and bash as her shell, add her to the accounting group without removing any other groups she has, and check the result. Explain why the method you chose avoids last month's mistake.
2. Give the commands to set the ownership and permissions on /srv/accounts so that only root and accounting members can use it, new files inherit the accounting group, and users cannot delete each other's files. State the numeric mode and explain what each part does.
3. Choose a umask that lets group members edit each other's new files while giving others no access. State the resulting permissions for new files and new directories, and say where you would set it so that it lasts beyond the current session.
4. Explain how to make sure sshd runs now and after a reboot, and how to block direct root login over SSH, including what you must do after editing the configuration file.
subParts: Create user and add to group
Enable SSH and block root login
modelAnswer: Create the account with: useradd -m -s /bin/bash priya (-m creates the home directory /home/priya, -s sets her login shell to bash), then set a password with: passwd priya. Add her to the group with: usermod -aG accounting priya. Check it with: groups priya, which should list accounting along with her primary group. The key detail is -a (append). Used with -G, it adds accounting to her existing supplementary groups. Running usermod -G accounting priya without -a replaces the entire supplementary-group list with just accounting, and that is exactly how last month's user lost their other memberships. Also note that a user who is already logged in only picks up a new group membership at their next login.

Run: chown root:accounting /srv/accounts so the directory is owned by root with group owner accounting. Then run: chmod 3770 /srv/accounts. In the first digit, 3 = 2 (SGID) + 1 (sticky). SGID makes every new file created inside take the accounting group instead of the creator's personal primary group, which fixes the problem of colleagues being unable to open each other's files. The sticky bit means only a file's owner, the directory owner (root), or root can delete or rename a file, which prevents accidental deletion of a coworker's spreadsheet. The second digit, 7, gives the owner (root) rwx. The third digit, 7, gives the accounting group rwx, so members can enter the folder and create, read, and edit files in it. The last digit, 0, gives others no access at all, so non-accountants are locked out. ls -ld /srv/accounts would show drwxrws--T. The lowercase s marks SGID on group execute, and the capital T marks the sticky bit with no execute permission for others.

Use umask 007. It removes nothing from the owner and group and removes all of r, w, and x from others. New files become 666 minus 007 = 660 (rw-rw----), so group members can read and edit them while others get nothing. New directories become 777 minus 007 = 770 (rwxrwx---). Typing umask 007 at the prompt only lasts for that shell session. To make it permanent for a user, put umask 007 in a shell startup file such as ~/.bashrc or ~/.profile. To apply it system-wide, put it in a global file such as /etc/profile or a script in /etc/profile.d/. A common mistake is to think the umask adds permissions. It only takes them away, so the old umask of 022 removed group write, and that is why files were coming out as 644.

Run: systemctl enable --now sshd. Enable makes the service start automatically at boot, and --now also starts it immediately. On some distributions the service is named ssh instead of sshd. Confirm it with: systemctl status sshd, which should show it as active and enabled. To block direct root login, edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set the line PermitRootLogin no. Then run systemctl restart sshd (or reload), because the daemon only reads its configuration file when it starts or reloads, so the edit has no effect until you do this. Keep your current session open and test a new login in a separate window first, so a configuration error cannot lock you out. Admins then log in as their own user and use sudo when they need root powers, which keeps a record of who did what and takes away the attacker's easiest target, the root account.

scenarios.title: Uploads Fail on a Disk That Looks Half Empty
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Freight Tools is a small, fictional logistics software company. Its order-tracking web app runs on one Linux server called track01. At 09:10 the support desk reports that customers can still view pages, but every file upload fails. The app's own error log shows this line: cannot create /var/spool/larkapp/session-88213.tmp: No space left on device.

You connect to track01 with SSH, a secure remote shell for running commands on another machine. Your team's runbook, a written step-by-step procedure, lists a troubleshooting method in this order: identify the problem and gather facts, form a theory of the likely cause, test the theory, plan and carry out a fix, verify the whole system works, then document what happened.

You run df -h. The df command reports how much of each file system is used, and -h prints human-readable sizes such as G for gigabytes. A file system is the structure that organises files on a disk partition. The line for /var shows Size 50G, Used 21G, Avail 29G, Use% 42%.

You then run df -i, where -i reports inodes instead of bytes. An inode is a small record that the file system keeps for every file and directory. It stores the owner, the permissions and where the data sits on disk, but not the file's name or contents. Most common Linux file systems create a fixed number of inodes when they are first set up, and every new file needs one free inode. The /var line shows Inodes 3,276,800, IUsed 3,276,800, IFree 0, IUse% 100%.

A colleague says: df says 29G is free, so this must be a bug in the app. Let's just restart it and see.

You keep investigating. The command find /var/spool/larkapp -type f | wc -l lists every regular file in that folder (find searches a directory tree, and -type f limits it to ordinary files). It then counts the lines (wc -l counts lines of text). The result is 3,104,552. Most of the files are named session-NNNN.tmp, and many are weeks old.

Next you run journalctl -u larkapp-cleanup. The journalctl tool reads the systemd journal, the central log that most modern distributions keep, and -u filters it to one unit. A unit is a service or job that systemd manages. A systemd timer, a scheduled trigger similar to a cron job, starts larkapp-cleanup every night at 02:00 to delete old session files. For each of the last 12 nights the journal shows: larkapp-cleanup.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'. The same output also shows, 12 days ago, the error: /usr/local/bin/larkclean: Permission denied.

One more fact: a command such as rm /var/spool/larkapp/*.tmp makes the shell expand the wildcard into every matching filename on a single command line. With millions of files, that can fail with Argument list too long. By contrast, find /var/spool/larkapp -name 'session-*.tmp' -mtime +1 -delete removes matching files older than one day, one at a time, without building one huge command line.

1. Explain why your colleague's plan does not follow the systematic method, and say which runbook step you are on when you run df -i.
2. Using the df -h and df -i output, state the root cause and explain why the error says no space when 29G is free.
3. Using the find count and the journal entries, explain how this problem built up over time.
4. Describe a safe immediate fix and a lasting fix, name one mistake to avoid while cleaning up, and say how you would verify the result.
subParts: Critique the restart plan and place df -i in the method
Identify the root cause from df output
Explain how the problem built up using logs
Fix, mistake to avoid, and verification
modelAnswer: The colleague is jumping to a fix before forming and testing a theory. That is guesswork, not the systematic method. A restart does not delete any files, so the inodes would still be full and uploads would fail again straight away. The team would also lose time and might wrongly blame the app. When you run df -i, you are testing a theory. The error says no space, df -h shows plenty of bytes free, so you suspect inode exhaustion and check it directly. Running df -h first was part of gathering facts.

The root cause is inode exhaustion on the /var file system. df -i shows IFree 0 and IUse% 100%, so no inodes are left. Every new file needs one free inode, so creating session-88213.tmp fails. Linux reports this with the same No space left on device message it uses for a full disk. df -h only counts bytes of data, and there are 29G of those free. The disk has room for data but has run out of the records needed to create new files, so both checks are needed to see the full picture.

The nightly larkapp-cleanup job, started by a systemd timer at 02:00, is supposed to delete old session files. The journal shows it has failed every night for 12 days, and the first failure says Permission denied when running /usr/local/bin/larkclean. That most likely means the script lost its execute permission or the job's access was changed. Since then, the app has kept creating small .tmp session files while nothing removed them. Each file used one inode. The count grew to about 3.1 million files and used up all 3,276,800 inodes. The files are tiny, which is why byte usage stayed at only 42%.

Immediate fix: run find /var/spool/larkapp -name 'session-*.tmp' -mtime +1 -delete. This removes only session files older than one day, one at a time, so active sessions are left alone. Mistake to avoid: do not use rm /var/spool/larkapp/*.tmp. The shell expands the wildcard into millions of names and the command can fail with Argument list too long. It would also delete current sessions that the app is still using. Lasting fix: correct the Permission denied error on /usr/local/bin/larkclean (for example, restore its execute permission or the correct owner), then run the larkapp-cleanup service once by hand. Verify: check journalctl -u larkapp-cleanup shows the job finishing without errors. Check that df -i for /var now shows a healthy number of free inodes. Confirm with the support desk that an upload works. Check df -i again after the next 02:00 run to make sure the count stays low. Finally, document the cause and fix, and consider an alert on inode usage as well as disk space.

scenarios.title: Hardening a new web server at Larkspur Freight
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Freight, a small fictional shipping company, has just installed a fresh Linux server called web01. It will host the public website that customers use to track parcels. Before it goes live, your team lead asks you to do a baseline hardening pass. Hardening means switching off or locking down anything the server does not need, so an attacker has fewer ways in.

Here is what you find. SSH, the encrypted remote-login service that admins use to reach the server's shell, still lets anyone log in as root (the all-powerful administrator account) and still accepts plain passwords. Your own public key, the shareable half of a key pair whose private half stays only on your laptop, is already installed for your normal account, priya. A contractor account called deploy has been given full sudo rights. Sudo is the tool that lets an ordinary user run a command as root, and "full rights" means deploy can run any command as root, even though deploy only ever needs to restart the web server program, nginx. The host firewall, the packet filter running on the server itself, is managed by firewalld, a front end that groups rules into zones. Right now it allows several services nobody uses. The website only needs SSH on port 22 and HTTPS on port 443. HTTPS is web traffic protected by TLS, the encryption that secures data while it is in transit.

Finally, a colleague copied the website files into a new directory, /srv/site. Nginx returns "403 Forbidden" for every page, even though the ordinary Unix permissions let nginx read the files. SELinux is in enforcing mode on this server. SELinux is a mandatory access control (MAC) system: on top of normal file permissions, it attaches a label called a security context to every process and file, and it blocks any access that its policy does not explicitly allow. The colleague suggests simply turning SELinux off.

1. Describe the SSH configuration changes you would make, how you would apply them without locking yourself out, and what each change defends against.
2. Describe how you would reduce the deploy account's sudo rights to only what it needs, how you would edit the rule safely, and why this matters.
3. Describe the firewalld changes that leave only SSH and HTTPS reachable, how you would make them survive a reboot, and what this protects against.
4. Explain why nginx is being blocked even though the file permissions look correct, give the proper fix instead of disabling SELinux, and say why disabling it would be a mistake.
subParts: SSH key-only auth and no root login
Firewall: allow only SSH and HTTPS
modelAnswer:
In the SSH server's configuration file (/etc/ssh/sshd_config, or a file under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/), set PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no and PubkeyAuthentication yes. On many systems you should also make sure KbdInteractiveAuthentication (older name ChallengeResponseAuthentication) is set to no, so passwords cannot sneak back in another way.

To avoid a lockout, apply the change carefully. First confirm that key login already works for priya. Then check the file's syntax with sshd -t. Reload the service with systemctl reload sshd (on Debian or Ubuntu the service is called ssh). Keep your current session open while you test a brand-new login from a second terminal, and only close the old session once the new one succeeds.

What each change defends against: turning off password logins defeats brute-force and password-guessing attacks, and stops stolen or reused passwords from working, because an attacker would also need the private key. Turning off direct root login means attackers cannot aim straight at the one account name that exists on every Linux system and has full power. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo instead, which also leaves a record of who did what.

Edit sudo rules only with visudo, for example visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy. Visudo checks the syntax before saving, so a typo cannot break sudo for everyone. Remove deploy from any group that has full rights (such as wheel or sudo), or delete the existing ALL rule for it. Replace it with a rule that allows a single command, for example: deploy ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx. Always use the full path to the command. Then confirm the result with sudo -l -U deploy.

This follows least privilege, which means giving each account only the access its job requires. If the contractor's account or credentials are ever compromised, the attacker can restart nginx and nothing more. They cannot read secrets, add users or install malware as root. It also lowers the damage from honest mistakes.

Check which zone is active and what it allows with firewall-cmd --get-active-zones and firewall-cmd --list-all. Add the needed services permanently with firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh and firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https. Remove every unneeded service, for example firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=dhcpv6-client and the same for cockpit or any other extras, along with any opened ports listed under ports. Then run firewall-cmd --reload and check the result with --list-all.

The --permanent flag writes the rule to saved configuration so it survives a reboot. The reload makes the saved rules take effect now. Without --permanent, a change applies only until the next reload or reboot. Make sure ssh stays allowed before you reload, or you will cut off your own remote session.

What this protects against: incoming traffic that does not match an allowed service is rejected. Only the two services the server actually needs can be reached from the network. This shrinks the attack surface, so a forgotten or vulnerable service cannot be reached even if it is accidentally left running.

SELinux checks labels as well as normal permissions, and both checks must pass. Files copied into a new directory like /srv/site get a generic label, often default_t or var_t, instead of the web-content type httpd_sys_content_t. SELinux policy does not allow the web server's process type (httpd_t) to read files with that generic label, so access is denied even though the rwx permissions allow it. You can confirm this in two ways. Run ls -Z /srv/site to see the labels. Look for denial records, called AVC denials, in the audit log with ausearch -m avc -ts recent.

The proper fix is to teach SELinux the correct label for the path and then apply it. Run semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/site(/.*)?" to record the rule, then restorecon -Rv /srv/site to relabel the existing files. Recording the rule with semanage means the label survives a future relabel. A plain chcon would be lost.

Disabling SELinux, or putting it in permissive mode with setenforce 0, would remove the protection for the whole server just to fix one directory. SELinux limits what a compromised process can touch. If nginx were exploited, SELinux would stop it from reading files like /etc/shadow or users' home directories, or writing outside its allowed areas, even if the normal permissions would allow it. Turning it off hides the real problem and throws that containment away.

scenarios.title: Nightly Config Backup at Bramblewick Bakeries
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Bramblewick Bakeries, a fictional regional bakery chain, as a junior Linux administrator. Their order system runs on one Linux server called oven01. Its settings live in several configuration files (plain-text files that control how a program behaves) ending in .conf inside the directory /etc/ovenctl. Last month someone edited one of those files by mistake and nobody had a copy of the old version. Your team lead wants a nightly backup that runs on its own, with no person typing commands.

Here is what you need to know. A Bash script is a plain-text file of shell commands that the computer runs from top to bottom. Its first line, #!/bin/bash, is called the shebang. It tells Linux which program should run the file.

A variable is a named box that holds a value. You create one with NAME=value, with no spaces on either side of the equals sign. You read it back with $NAME. Wrap it in double quotes, as in "$NAME", so that a path containing spaces stays in one piece. A common mistake is writing NAME = value with spaces. Bash then treats NAME as a command to run, prints an error, and the variable is never set. Writing $(command) is called command substitution: Bash runs the command and drops its output into that spot. For example, $(date +%F) becomes today's date, such as 2025-03-14.

A conditional runs commands only when a test is true. It is written as if [ test ]; then commands; fi. The test -d path is true when that directory exists. Putting ! in front reverses the test, so [ ! -d "$DIR" ] means the directory does not exist. The command mkdir -p creates a directory and any missing parent directories.

A for loop repeats commands once for each item in a list. It is written as for item in list; do commands; done. The pattern /etc/ovenctl/*.conf expands to every file ending in .conf in that directory. The command cp copies a file. Writing echo text >> file adds a line of text to the end of a file.

Cron is the Linux scheduler that runs commands at set times. Each user has a crontab (cron table), which you edit with crontab -e. Each line in it has five time fields followed by the command to run. In order, the fields are minute (0-59), hour (0-23 on a 24-hour clock), day of month, month, and day of week. A * in a field means every value. Cron starts jobs with very few settings and does not know which directory you were working in. For that reason you should always give the full path to the script. The script must also be executable, which you allow with chmod +x file.

The grep command prints the lines of a file that match a regular expression (a text pattern). Inside a pattern, ^ means the start of a line. So '^ERROR' matches only lines that begin with ERROR. The -c option makes grep print a count of matching lines instead of the lines themselves.

Git is a version control tool that records snapshots of files over time, so you can see what changed and roll back. You use git add file to stage a file, which marks it for the next snapshot. You then use git commit -m "message" to save the snapshot with a short description. Your team keeps all scripts in a git repository (a folder that git tracks) at /opt/admin-scripts.

Your tasks:
1. Write the script /opt/admin-scripts/backup-ovenctl.sh. It must set variables for the source directory /etc/ovenctl, a destination of /srv/backups/ovenctl/ followed by today's date, and a log file /var/log/ovenctl-backup.log. It must use a conditional to create the destination directory if it does not exist. It must use a for loop to copy every .conf file and write one line to the log for each file copied.
2. Write the exact crontab line that runs this script every day at 2:30 a.m., and name one thing you must do so that cron can actually run it.
3. The backup log also receives lines written by other tools. Write a single command that prints how many lines in /var/log/ovenctl-backup.log begin with the word ERROR, and explain what the ^ does.
4. Write the two git commands, run from inside /opt/admin-scripts, that save the new script into version control with a sensible message.

A correct script:
#!/bin/bash
SRC_DIR="/etc/ovenctl"
DEST_DIR="/srv/backups/ovenctl/$(date +%F)"
LOG="/var/log/ovenctl-backup.log"
if [ ! -d "$DEST_DIR" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$DEST_DIR"
fi
for f in "$SRC_DIR"/*.conf; do
  cp "$f" "$DEST_DIR/"
  echo "copied $f" >> "$LOG"
done

Grading points: the shebang line is present. There are three variables assigned with no spaces around the equals sign. The destination uses $(date +%F), so each day's backup gets its own folder and earlier backups are not overwritten. The conditional uses [ ! -d ... ] with mkdir -p. The for loop goes over the .conf files and does one cp and one echo >> to the log per file. Variables are read with $ and quoted. Equivalent wording, such as a different loop variable name or a different log message, is acceptable.

30 2 * * * /opt/admin-scripts/backup-ovenctl.sh

The fields mean minute 30, hour 2, every day of the month, every month, and every day of the week. Acceptable "one thing" answers: make the script executable with chmod +x /opt/admin-scripts/backup-ovenctl.sh, or use the full absolute path in the crontab line because cron does not know your working directory. A reply that adds it with crontab -e is also good. Common wrong answers are 2 30 * * * (fields reversed, which is invalid because hour 30 does not exist) or 30 14 * * * (that is 2:30 p.m.).

grep -c '^ERROR' /var/log/ovenctl-backup.log

The ^ anchors the pattern to the start of the line. Only lines that begin with ERROR are counted, and lines that merely contain the word ERROR somewhere in the middle are not. The -c option prints the number of matching lines instead of the lines themselves.

git add backup-ovenctl.sh
git commit -m "Add nightly backup script for ovenctl config files"

git add stages the file, meaning it marks the file to be included in the next snapshot. git commit records that snapshot with a short description of what changed and why. Any clear, descriptive message is acceptable. Committing without staging first, or using an empty or meaningless message, does not fully meet the task.
